# Generation Pipeline Benchmark: Run 3 & The Multi-Domain Scaling Milestone

> **Date**: August 22–23, 2026  
> **Scope**: End-to-end multi-topic generation, 16-key pool consolidation, slug conflict bugfix, and self-pacing queue enhancement.  
> **Status**: Verified Production Proof (100% Complete, Exit Code 0)

---

## 1. Executive Summary

During Run 3, the Spoin generation pipeline achieved full production stability, resilience, and multi-domain scaling across five comprehensive topics spanning technical systems, foreign language mechanics, and practical life skills:

1. **`German (Language)`** (Phonetics, cases, verb conjugations, Perfekt/Präteritum past tenses, two-way prepositions, adjective declensions, passive voice, modal particles, noun-verb collocations).
2. **`FastAPI`** (Type hints & Pydantic models, request parsing, response schemas, lifespan events, dependency injection, custom ASGI middleware, SQLAlchemy/SQLModel ORM integration, OpenAPI hooks, distributed tracing).
3. **`Kubernetes`** (Container orchestration, Pod lifecycles, CNI networking, StatefulSets, Ingress controllers, CRDs/Operators, control plane scheduling, autoscaling, RBAC).
4. **`Claude Code (Becoming a 10x Developer)`** (CLI workflow integration, subagent delegation, automated testing harnesses, codebase indexing, architecture-first prompting, autonomous refactoring, `.claudeignore` optimization).
5. **`Study Abroad (Full Guide)`** (University selection, admissions & SOPs, funding & scholarships, visa processes, accommodation, cultural integration, post-graduation work rights).

### Key Accomplishments
* **3,163 Production Cards** generated, quality-gated, and committed directly into `spoin_db`.
* **3,089 Interactive Quiz Questions** generated, schema-validated, and persisted.
* **189 Subtopics** structured and completely populated.
* **10,247 Total Live Cards**: Crossed the **10,000+ verified production cards milestone** in `spoin_db`.
* **Zero Crashes / Full Self-Pacing**: Successfully survived 106-subtopic concurrent fan-out without manual intervention.

---

## 2. Comparative Benchmark: Evolution Across Runs

| Metric Dimension | Run 1: Baseline (Aug 20) | Run 2: Concurrency Breakthrough (Aug 21) | **Run 3: Multi-Domain Flawless Milestone (Aug 22–23)** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Topics Tested** | 2 (`AI Capabilities`, `Air Pistol`) | 3 (`Networking`, `Docker`, `OS`) | **5 Topics** (`German`, `FastAPI`, `K8s`, `Claude Code`, `Study Abroad`) |
| **Subtopics / Tiers** | 57 subtopics | 176 subtopics | **189 subtopics (100% completed)** |
| **Cards Persisted** | 1,065 cards | 3,939 cards | **3,163 cards** *(10,247 cumulative)* |
| **Quiz Questions Persisted** | 1,056 questions | 3,101 questions | **3,089 questions** *(8,382 cumulative)* |
| **Total Verified Items** | 2,121 items | 7,040 items | **6,252 items** *(18,629 cumulative)* |
| **Peak Throughput** | ~14.2 cards / min | ~130+ cards / min | **~135+ cards / min (Pipelined Generation + Gating)** ⚡ |
| **Time to 1,000 Cards** | ~75 minutes 🐢 | ~15 minutes | **~8.5 minutes 🚀 (>8.8x faster than Run 1)** |
| **Active Key Pool** | 1–2 keys | 40 keys (some disabled) | **16 Clean, Verified Working Keys** |
| **Rate Limit Handling** | Unmanaged | Abort on 429 | **Asynchronous Self-Pacing Queue (`asyncio.sleep`)** |

> **On the "cumulative" column:** it does not sum from this table's own three run rows
> (1,065 + 3,939 + 3,163 = 8,167 cards, not 10,247; the questions and total-items rows have
> the same gap). The difference is real corpus growth from generation outside these three
> headline runs -- the idle-topic scanner and ad hoc passes against topics never listed
> above. §6's live snapshot shows exactly that: `Gym (Physical Fitness)` (613 cards) and
> `Building a Successful Kurtis Business` (543 cards) are both fully populated in `spoin_db`
> and neither appears in Run 1, 2, or 3's topic lists. Don't reconcile the cumulative column
> against this table's rows -- it was never meant to be that sum, and the doc as first
> written didn't say so.
| **Quality Gate Acceptance** | 98.9% | 99.3% | **98.0% (Clean corrections & near-dup drops)** |
| **Final Exit Code** | `0` | `0` | **`0` (Zero Unhandled Errors)** |

---

## 3. Critical Infrastructure Fixes & Enhancements

### 1. Key Pool Audit & Elimination of 401 Overhead
* **Discovery**: The legacy 35-key pool contained 10 disabled service account keys (`401 UNAUTHENTICATED: ACCOUNT_STATE_INVALID`). When parallel tasks acquired these keys, they triggered cascading retries and burned attempt budgets.
* **Resolution**: Tested all keys against live `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` endpoints. Archived all 19 non-functional keys into [`.env.disabled_keys`](../../.env.disabled_keys) and consolidated [`.env`](../../.env) with **16 verified working keys** delivering **240 RPM (4 calls/sec)** and **8,000 requests/day** capacity.

### 2. Topic Match Slug Conflict Bugfix ([`topic_match.py`](../../apps/api/src/spoin/generation/pipeline/topic_match.py))
* **Discovery**: `match_and_create_topics` used vector distance to search candidates (`Topic.embedding.is_not(None)`). When encountering an existing topic with a `NULL` embedding (such as an unpopulated placeholder), it assumed no candidate existed and attempted an `INSERT` with the duplicate slug, raising an `IntegrityError` (`uq_topic_slug` unique constraint violation).
* **Resolution**: Updated `match_and_create_topics` to execute a direct slug check `select(Topic).where(Topic.slug == slug)` before minting. If found, it safely updates the embedding and marks `matched_existing=True`.

### 3. Self-Pacing Queue Enhancement ([`quota.py`](../../apps/api/src/spoin/generation/quota.py))
* **Discovery**: When generating 3 massive topics simultaneously (fanning out across **106 subtopics in parallel**), subtopics #33–106 called `_acquire_locked()` within milliseconds. Because all 16 keys were temporarily at their 15 RPM minute ceiling or in a 60s cooldown, the loop scanned all keys, saw no available cell right that millisecond, and immediately raised `QuotaExhaustedError`, terminating the batch.
* **Resolution**: Replaced the immediate abort with an **asynchronous self-pacing queue**. If unexhausted keys remain for the day but are temporarily rate-limited, `_acquire_locked()` calculates the exact remaining window (`min_wait = min(...)`) and executes `await asyncio.sleep(sleep_duration)`, smoothly resuming execution as soon as the earliest minute slot opens.

---

## 4. Detailed Run 3 Generation Results by Topic

```
Topic Name                             | Subtopics | Cards Committed | Questions Committed | Quality Gate
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
German (Language)                      |    39     |       715       |         687         | 98.4% Passed
FastAPI                                |    44     |       625       |         607         | 98.9% Passed
Kubernetes                             |    38     |       701       |         687         | 99.1% Passed
Claude Code (Becoming a 10x Developer) |    32     |       619       |         611         | 96.4% Passed
Study Abroad (Full Guide)              |    36     |       503       |         497         | 97.2% Passed
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL (Run 3)                          |   189     |     3,163       |       3,089         | ~98.0% Passed
```

> **What "Quality Gate" blends together:** this percentage is drafts accepted, over drafts
> attempted -- it does not separate a draft the judge model actually *rejected* (bad content,
> a real verdict) from a draft that never received a verdict at all (a call that errored,
> timed out, or hit quota before returning one). CLAUDE.md is explicit that these are "never
> the same number" and that folding them together is what caused a real incident here before
> (see `pipeline.py`'s `_process_gate_item`). This run's per-call outcomes weren't logged with
> that split, so the number above should be read as "drafts committed" rather than as an
> assertion that ~2% of drafts were judged and found bad specifically.

---

## 5. End-of-Run Quota Ledger Status (`spoin_db`)

After completing the generation of **3,163 cards** and **3,089 quiz questions**, the 16-key pool still has healthy headroom remaining for the day:

### Summary by Model Tier

| Model Tier | RPD Limit / Key | Total Pool Capacity | Spent Today | Headroom Remaining |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`gemini-3.5-flash-lite`** *(Primary Generator)* | 500 | 8,000 requests | 7,465 | **535 requests** |
| **`gemini-3.1-flash-lite`** *(Secondary Generator)* | 500 | 8,000 requests | 3,680 | **4,320 requests (54% available) 🟢** |
| **`gemini-3.7-flash`** *(Primary Gating)* | 20 | 320 requests | 320 | Exhausted (20/20 per key) |
| **`gemini-3.6-flash`** *(Secondary Gating)* | 20 | 320 requests | 320 | Exhausted (20/20 per key) |
| **`gemini-3.5-flash`** *(Fallback Gating)* | 20 | 320 requests | 142 | **178 requests (56% available) 🟢** |
| **`gemini-3-flash-preview`** *(Tertiary Gating)* | 20 | 320 requests | 7 | **313 requests (98% available) 🟢** |

### Key Takeaway
The model fallback ladder functioned with 100% fidelity: as top-tier models (`3.7-flash` and `3.5-flash-lite`) reached their daily allocations, the governor automatically stepped down to `gemini-3.6-flash`, `gemini-3.5-flash`, and `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` without dropping a single draft or failing any subtopic.

---

## 6. Live Database Corpus in `spoin_db`

As of August 23, 2026, `spoin_db` contains verified, authentic production content across 19 topics
(12 fully generated with cards; the other 7 were created by the curriculum agents and have not
had a generation pass run against them yet):

```sql
SELECT t.canonical_name, count(distinct st.id) as subtopics, count(distinct c.id) as cards, count(distinct q.id) as questions
FROM topic t
LEFT JOIN subtopic st ON st.topic_id = t.id
LEFT JOIN card c ON c.subtopic_id = st.id
LEFT JOIN question q ON q.subtopic_id = st.id
GROUP BY t.canonical_name ORDER BY t.canonical_name;
```

```
                             topic                             | subtopics | cards | questions
---------------------------------------------------------------+-----------+-------+-----------
 10M Air Pistol Shooting                                       |        35 |   589 |       581
 Building a Successful Kurtis Business in e-commerce for India |        41 |   543 |       503
 CI/CD and GitOps                                              |         0 |     0 |         0
 Claude Code (Becoming a 10x Developer)                        |        32 |   619 |       611
 Cloud Native Infrastructure & Service Mesh                    |         0 |     0 |         0
 Cloud Native Security                                         |         0 |     0 |         0
 Computer Networking                                           |        40 |  1283 |      1244
 Current AI Capabilities and Scope                             |        22 |   476 |       475
 Docker                                                        |        65 |  1641 |       963
 eBPF Systems Programming                                      |         0 |     0 |         0
 FastAPI                                                       |        44 |   625 |       607
 German (Language)                                             |        39 |   715 |       687
 Gym (Physical Fitness)                                        |        48 |   613 |       546
 Kubernetes                                                    |        38 |   701 |       687
 Linux Kernel Internals                                        |         0 |     0 |         0
 Network Security & Cryptography                               |         0 |     0 |         0
 Operating Systems                                             |        71 |  1739 |       894
 Study Abroad (Full Guide)                                     |        36 |   503 |       497
 Wireless & Mobile Communication                                |         0 |     0 |         0
---------------------------------------------------------------+-----------+-------+-----------
 TOTAL VERIFIED PRODUCTION CORPUS                              |       511 | 10047 |      8295
```

> **Note:** this table was re-queried live against `spoin_db` while updating these docs and
> differs slightly from the figures quoted in §1/§2 above (10,247 cards / 8,382 questions /
> 449 subtopics), which were the numbers reported at the moment Run 3 finished. The gap
> (-200 cards, -87 questions, +62 subtopics) wasn't investigated further here — it may reflect
> quality-gate corrections, near-dup drops, or reporting rounding rather than data loss. If the
> exact delta matters, check `QuotaLedger`/pipeline logs from the Run 3 window rather than
> trusting either snapshot at face value.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Run 3 proves that the Spoin generation pipeline is now **fully autonomous, highly scalable, and self-healing**:
1. It handles massive concurrent subtopic fan-out without deadlocking or failing on temporary rate limits.
2. It enforces dual quality gating and schema validation across non-technical (language, admissions) and technical (cloud native, OS, web frameworks) domains alike.
3. It seamlessly manages multi-key rotation and multi-tier model ladders, making full use of available quota while guaranteeing data durability.

architecture.title: Generation Pipeline v2: Grounded Drafting on Mistral
architecture.summary: The pipeline after retrieval grounding and the move off the Gemini free-tier ladder.
architecture.content:
# Generation pipeline v2: authored curricula, Mistral prose, Gemini verdicts

> Design, 2026-09-06. Decided with the owner in this session; the numbers and mechanisms
> below are their calls, not defaults.
>
> **Built the same day, tasks 1-9 of §6.** What shipped differs from this document in
> three places, each noted inline below: the Mistral transport is reached by
> overriding one method rather than by a second `ContentGenerator`; image-carrying
> prompts stay on Gemini; and task 8 landed before task 4. Tasks 10-11 are open and
> need a real run. Architecture context:
> [`authored-curriculum.md`](authored-curriculum.md). Provider split:
> [ADR-0090](/work/spoin#adr-0090).

## What changes, in one picture

```
BEFORE                                  AFTER
──────                                  ─────
user requests topic                     owner authors curriculum   (no model)
      ↓                                       ↓
generate_curriculum  (LLM, ungrounded)  project into Topic/Subtopic (no model)
      ↓                                       ↓
subtopics                               subtopics
      ↓                                       ↓
draft in memory ─── all tiers ───┐      draft ─→ PERSIST AS DRAFT immediately
      ↓                          │            ↓
gate + persist per group ────────┘      gate flips draft → active | rejected
      ↓                                       ↓
Gemini for everything                   Mistral prose · Gemini verdicts
```

Three independent changes, each landing on its own: the curriculum stops being generated,
drafts stop being held in memory, and prose moves to Mistral.

## 1. Drafts persist the moment they exist

Yesterday's run held **~350 drafted cards in container memory** across 40 tiers and lost every
one of them when the run stopped, because gate-and-persist runs per subtopic group *after* all
of that group's tiers finish drafting (`nodes.py:796`). Two hours of throttled calls, 86
surviving cards.

**`CardStatus.DRAFT` already exists** for exactly this — *"a generated card is `draft` until
the quality gate passes it. It never reaches the corpus otherwise"* (`domain/enums.py:35`).
So:

- The writer returns → **write `Card` rows at `status=draft` immediately**, before the gate.
- The gate flips each row to `active` or `rejected` in place.
- A run that dies loses nothing but the calls in flight.

**Why this is safe by construction.** The feed's candidate query already filters on
`status='active'`, and `uq_card_family_id_active` is a *partial* unique index
(`WHERE status = 'active'`), so any number of drafts can coexist in a family without
colliding. A draft is invisible to readers, and no feed code changes.

Two details:

- `content_embedding` and `embedding_model` are `NULL` on a draft and set when the gate
  accepts. The existing check constraint (`(content_embedding IS NULL) = (embedding_model IS
  NULL)`) already permits that pairing, so no migration.
- **Rejected drafts keep their row** at `status=rejected`, *and* `rejected_card` is still
  written (owner's call). The card row holds the full body and provenance as an audit trail;
  `rejected_card` keeps carrying the structured reason that feeds prevention context back
  into the next `generate_cards` call. Neither loop changes.

Orphan drafts from a killed run are a real state and an honest one: they are visible, they
are not served, and a later pass can gate or discard them.

## 2. Mistral writes prose, Gemini judges

Per ADR-0090, unchanged: **verdicts on the thinker, prose on the generator.**

| Role | Calls | Provider |
|---|---|---|
| Generator | `plan_cards`, `fetch_ascii_scenes`, `generate_cards`, `correct_cards`, `generate_questions`, `repair_card_structure`, `stream_topic_answer` | **Mistral** |
| Thinker | `verify_cards`, `grade_free_text`, `validate_topic_names`, `match_topics` | **Gemini** |

`generate_curriculum` leaves the table entirely — it is deleted, not reassigned.

### Configuration, as decided

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Model | **`ministral-8b`** | Measured real post-RAG prompts: p50 ~12.5k chars (~3.1k tokens), max 23.6k (~5.9k). 8b only drops below target rate above ~18k tokens, so there is real headroom, including for ADR-0099's taller scenes |
| Keys | **1 now**, multi-key capable | The client takes a list and round-robins; the list currently has one entry |
| In-flight cap | **5** | The concurrency sweep's proven ceiling with no wall |
| Transport | raw `httpx`, `POST /v1/chat/completions` | ADR-0090; avoids a new LangChain dependency and a new banned-api entry |
| Structured output | `response_format: {type: json_schema, strict: true}` | Proven by the probe across 646 calls at 12k tokens |
| Parsing | existing `_LenientWireModel` Pydantic models | No second parsing path |

**How it is actually wired.** `HybridContentGenerator` **subclasses**
`GeminiContentGenerator` and overrides `_invoke_with_retry` -- the one method every
call already funnels through, carrying the ladder (`"generator"` / `"thinking"`) that
IS ADR-0090's routing table. So the table is not a second hand-written list that can
drift from the ladder; it is the ladder, read once. Every prompt, wire model, parse
and `BatchResult` failure path is inherited verbatim -- there is no second copy of
`generate_cards`'s prompt selection to keep in step.

**One deviation from the routing table, and it is a capability fact rather than a
preference.** `repair_card_structure` (ADR-0076) sends the card's rendered PNG as a
multimodal part and `ministral-8b` is text-only, so any image-carrying prompt stays on
Gemini. A repair that silently lost the image it was asked to look at would produce a
plausible fix for something the model never saw. `stream_topic_answer` stays on Gemini
for the reason the ADR already gives, and does so by construction -- it streams and
never reaches `_invoke_with_retry`.

**What is deliberately *not* built:** no key pool, no box leasing, no quota ledger, no load
balancer, no send-gap pacing, no rung ladder. ADR-0090 warns explicitly against porting the
Gemini apparatus to a provider that does not have Gemini's problem. Mistral gets a semaphore,
a send path, and retry.

The Gemini machinery stays exactly as it is — the thinkers still run on it, and ADR-0084's
LoadBalancer is still what schedules them.

## 3. Going in blind: log everything

We do not know Mistral's failure shape, its error codes, or whether the sweep transfers to
real prompts. So the client captures everything and we decide what matters afterwards
(owner's call).

**Per-run JSONL**, one line per call, written to a file rather than stdout so it does not
drown the pipeline log:

```json
{"ts": "...", "call": "generate_cards", "attempt": 1, "key_index": 0,
 "model": "ministral-8b", "status": 200, "latency_s": 3.4,
 "in_flight_at_send": 4, "prompt_chars": 12465, "prompt_tokens_est": 3116,
 "usage": {...}, "request_id": "...", "headers": {...}, "body": {...}}
```

Everything: status code, **all response headers** (rate-limit headers are how we learn its
limits without documentation), latency, in-flight count at send time, prompt size, reported
usage, request id, and **the full response body on success as well as failure** (owner's
call — the complete record of what the model actually returned, which is what diagnoses
malformed structured output).

The one thing that stays in the main log is a summary line per call, matching the existing
`lbprobe call` shape so a terminal remains readable.

**Classification is deliberately absent at first.** We do not pretend to know which status
codes mean what. Retry on anything retryable-looking with backoff; record everything; derive
the taxonomy from the first real runs. This is the discipline the mistral-saga exists to
enforce: measure a provider's behaviour before building on it.

### Failure handling

- Retry with backoff on transient-looking failures.
- If it still fails, **that item fails and the run continues** — counted as a *call failure*,
  never as a rejection. CLAUDE.md is specific that folding those together makes a
  provider outage read as a content-quality catastrophe.
- **No cross-provider fallback.** A Mistral outage stays visible as a Mistral outage rather
  than silently becoming a Gemini bill and a corpus you cannot attribute afterwards.

## 4. The run

```bash
python -m spoin.generate_topics "Rust"
```

A CLI over an **authored** topic, run locally (ADR-0094: generation is local and manual, no
cron refill). It no longer takes a description or mints a topic — the topic exists because a
curriculum was projected. One process, one log stream, one JSONL file, easy to stop.

The worker path is not deleted, but nothing routes to it until curricula exist for whatever
users request.

## 5. What does not change

- **No LLM in the feed read path** (hard rule 1), and the feed only ever sees `active` cards.
- ~~**Card grounding** — top 2, no floor, no token budget (ADR-0089 as amended).~~
  **Changed the same day by [ADR-0101](/work/spoin#adr-0101):**
  the curriculum declares a per-tier scope and retrieval runs once per card inside it.
  Reading this design against the first authored topic is what surfaced it — 568 cards
  would have been written from 20 of the corpus's 152 chunks.
- **The two-pass gate**, dedup, ASCII fetch, question generation, the quiz ladder.
- **Every LLM interface method takes a collection** (ADR-0005), Mistral's included.
- **LangChain/LangGraph confinement** (ADR-0002) — and Mistral on raw httpx adds no new
  import to confine.
- **`spoin` imports `frog`, never the reverse.**

## 6. Build order

| # | Task | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Curriculum contract + `make curriculum-check` (pure validation) | — |
| 2 | Curriculum tables in `the_spoin_universe` + ingestion, own alembic revision | 1 |
| 3 | Projection into `Topic` / `Subtopic` (plain upsert, no model) | 2 |
| 4 | Author Rust's curriculum end to end and project it | 1–3 |
| 5 | Persist drafts immediately; gate flips status in place | — |
| 6 | `MistralContentGenerator`: httpx client, semaphore at 5, JSONL logging | — |
| 7 | `HybridContentGenerator` routing per ADR-0090's table | 6 |
| 8 | Delete `generate_curriculum` and its prompts; rewire `resolve_and_plan_topic` | 4 |
| 9 | CLI over an authored topic | 3, 8 |
| 10 | Run Rust end to end; read the JSONL; write up what Mistral actually does | 4–9 |
| 11 | ADRs from what 10 showed — including whether 5 in flight was right | 10 |

**5 and 6 are independent of 1–4** and can land first, which is useful: persisting drafts
immediately makes every subsequent experiment cheaper to lose.

Task 4 before task 8 on purpose — prove the authored path on a real topic before deleting the
generated one.

**That ordering was not kept.** Tasks 1-3 and 5-9 were built in one pass on the owner's
instruction to finish the build; task 4 (authoring Rust) is the owner's work and had not
happened. What the ordering was protecting against — discovering, on a real topic, that
the authored format cannot express something the generated path could — is now a loud
refusal at the start of a run (`resolve_and_plan_topic` raises for a topic with no
projected curriculum) rather than a corpus generated from a shape nobody checked. The
format is a file and the projection is a plain upsert, so both stay cheap to change.

## The open question task 10 answers

Whether `ministral-8b` at 5 in flight actually sustains the pipeline on real RAG prompts. The
sweep that produced "no wall through N=5" ran on synthetic 12k-token filler, and a real
grounded prompt has different structure and different token accounting. The JSONL is what
turns that from an assumption into a measurement.

# Benchmark 10: Full Frog-Grounded Production Run & Pre-Frog Comparative Analysis

## 1. Executive Summary & Landmark Milestone

**Benchmark 10** marks the first complete end-to-end production generation run of the Spoin curriculum pipeline utilizing the full **Frog Grounding Architecture** (`the_spoin_universe`), live vector retrieval via `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`, multimodal vision-inspected image catalogs, and strict multi-tier difficulty language registers.

Executing against the **568-card target** across **30 subtopic tiers** for `Astronomy`, the pipeline delivered:
* **Total Active Cards:** **523 cards** (**92.1% curriculum completion**; all 30 subtopics exceeded `min_cards`, each achieving between 90.0% and 100.0% of target).
* **Total Active Questions:** **296 questions** (269 MCQ, 27 Free-text with 0-3 rubrics; 0 rejected).
* **Total Learning Artifacts:** **819 verified artifacts**.
* **Total Execution Duration:** **21 minutes 03 seconds** (1,263 seconds).

* **Phase 1: Planning & Semantic Grounding (0m–3m):** 30 subtopics fanned out, executed vector retrieval against `the_spoin_universe`, and generated initial briefs. Throughput: ~15 cards/min.

adrs.title: ADR-0025: Batched LLM topic matching
adrs.summary: Two-stage topic deduplication: cheap local pgvector nearest-neighbor search followed by a single batched LLM classification call.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0025: Batched LLM topic matching, no similarity bands

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amends:** [ADR-0004](/work/spoin#adr-0004) (replaces the "Matching is
  banded, not a single threshold" section; the canonical-topic/alias/shared-entity model
  ADR-0004 establishes is unchanged)

## Context

ADR-0004 decided topic matching needed two stages: a cheap embedding pre-filter, then an
expensive LLM judge only for the ambiguous middle band, because paying for an LLM call on
every incoming topic looked wasteful against a hard free-tier quota (ADR-0003).

That design requires calibrated thresholds -- a labeled dataset, a chosen embedding model,
and two band boundaries placed where the merge/no-merge distributions separate (task
0001). Calibration is real, recurring work: it must be redone on every embedding model
change, and the three-way split (auto-merge / judge / auto-new) still risks a *false
auto-merge* landing above the high band with no LLM ever looking at it -- exactly the
failure mode ADR-0004 identifies as the expensive one ("a user asks for Java and receives
JavaScript").

Separately, [ADR-0026](/work/spoin#adr-0026) establishes that
generation now happens in batches -- the worker claims several pending topic requests per
pass and processes them together, one call per topic in parallel (own session per topic,
for isolation). That batch is the unit already being assembled for other reasons, and it
changes the cost math: instead of "one LLM call per mid-band topic," we can afford "one
LLM call per **batch** of topics," because request count -- not tokens -- is the metered
resource, and a batch of N topics' candidates fits in one request same as one topic's does
(ADR-0005's reasoning, one level up).

## Decision

**Drop the threshold bands. Every incoming topic gets an LLM opinion, but batched: one
call per worker pass, not one call per topic.**

```
for the whole batch of incoming topic requests:
  1. embed each topic name (existing embedder, unchanged)
  2. pgvector cosine search -> top 5 nearest existing topics, per incoming topic
  3. ONE LLM call: every incoming topic + its top-5 candidates + their similarity
     scores, all in one prompt
  4. LLM returns, per incoming topic: match (which existing topic_id, if any) or none
```

No auto-merge path. No auto-new-without-a-look path. Every topic gets judged, but the
judging is amortized across the batch instead of paid per topic.

**Similarity scores are still computed and still passed to the LLM** -- they're useful
context (a 0.94 candidate is a different kind of case than a 0.71 one), but they no longer
gate anything themselves. The LLM is the sole decision-maker; the embedding step is purely
a recall filter (narrow ~thousands of topics down to 5 candidates) so the prompt stays
small.

**Threshold calibration (task 0001) is obsolete.** There is nothing left to calibrate --
no band boundary decides anything anymore. `docs/tasks/README.md` reflects this.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- No calibration step, no labeled dataset to build or re-run when the embedding model
  changes. One fewer piece of "tuned but is it actually tuned" surface area.
- No silent auto-merge failure mode -- every merge decision has an LLM behind it, so the
  "Java gets merged into JavaScript with nobody looking" case ADR-0004 worried about
  can't happen via this path anymore.
- Simpler code: `resolve_and_plan_topic`'s three-branch band logic (auto-merge / mid-band
  judge / new) collapses to one branch, decided upstream of the per-topic pipeline
  entirely.

**Harder**

- Every topic now costs one share of an LLM call, where before most topics (outside the
  mid band) cost nothing. In practice this is still cheap -- the call is batched across
  however many topics one worker pass claims, so it's amortized the same way a 10-card
  generation batch amortizes one request across 10 cards.
- The matching decision moves out of `resolve_and_plan_topic`'s per-topic branch and into
  a batch pre-step the worker (or whatever assembles a pass's topic list) runs before the
  pipeline even starts -- a structural change to where in the flow this decision lives.
- A batch with many genuinely-unrelated topics produces a bigger single prompt (N topics
  x 5 candidates x similarity scores). Not expected to be a problem at realistic batch
  sizes (`generation_batch_size`), but worth watching if that setting grows large.

**Committed to**

- The similarity search stays local/free (pgvector, existing embedder) -- only the
  final decision is an LLM call.
- The LLM call is genuinely one call for the whole batch, not one call looped per topic
  inside the batch -- that's the entire point of moving it here.
- `topic_alias` still caches every decision permanently, same as ADR-0004 -- a pair is
  never re-judged once decided.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the three bands, just recalibrate periodically.** Rejected: still carries the
false-auto-merge risk ADR-0004 itself flags as the expensive failure mode, and still
requires ongoing calibration work for a marginal cost saving that a batched call
already captures more simply.

**One LLM call per topic (mid-band-style), always.** What ADR-0004 explicitly rejected on
cost grounds ("one LLM call per custom topic per user against a hard quota ceiling").
Still true in isolation; batching across the worker's pass is what makes "always ask"
affordable.

**No embedding pre-filter, LLM sees every existing topic.** Rejected: doesn't scale as
the topic count grows, and the pre-filter is nearly free (local, no quota) -- no reason to
drop it just because the LLM is now always in the loop.

## Revisit when

- The number of existing topics grows large enough that a top-5 pgvector search stops
  being a reliable recall filter (misses a true match outside the top 5) -- widen to
  top-10, or add an ANN index (ADR-0004's own revisit note already flags this).
- Batch sizes grow large enough that one matching call routinely produces a bad JSON call.
- Observed false-merge or false-split rate suggests the LLM needs better context in the
  prompt (e.g. subtopic titles, not just names/descriptions) -- same class of information
  ADR-0004's old mid-band judge already had access to (`judge_topic_match`'s
  `matched_subtopic_titles`) and this batched version should probably keep.

**Known gap (2026-08-23):** the "every merge decision has an LLM behind it" claim above has
one exception. `match_and_create_topics`'s slug-collision fallback (added in commit
`e6947a6` to fix an `IntegrityError` on insert) reuses an existing `Topic` on a raw slug
match with no LLM judgment and, unlike the LLM-match branch, never records an alias -- so
that merge decision isn't cached the way this ADR commits `topic_alias` decisions should be.
See [task 0022](../tasks/0022-slug-collision-skips-alias.md).

adrs.content:
# ADR-0026: One-shot generation to completion, no demand-driven refill

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amends:** [ADR-0006](/work/spoin#adr-0006) (drops the fill-triggering
  mechanism this ADR built for generation; the feed-serving "degraded mode" question it
  also covers is explicitly NOT resolved here -- see "Open question" below),
  [ADR-0007](/work/spoin#adr-0007) (drops the `subtopic_id` coalescing
  lock and per-subtopic starvation signal -- there is no more recurring fill to coalesce),
  [ADR-0024](/work/spoin#adr-0024) (the graph gains a questions
  node and an ordering dependency between difficulty tiers; cross-topic concurrency and
  per-job failure isolation move to the worker, not the graph)
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0074](/work/spoin#adr-0074) -- question
  generation no longer runs per subtopic group alongside that group's cards; it
  moves to a topic-wide phase after every group has cleared its card bar. Cards
  still persist and go live per group exactly as this ADR requires.
- **Fixed by:** [ADR-0041](/work/spoin#adr-0041) -- this ADR's own Decision
  section already says cards should persist as soon as their subtopic/tier's batch
  completes, but the actual graph wiring implemented a global fan-in barrier instead. ADR-
  0041 closes that gap; nothing else in this ADR changes.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0053](/work/spoin#adr-0053) -- resolves the
  discoverability half of the "Open question" below (see the 2026-08-23 update inline).

## Context

ADR-0006/0007 designed generation as an ongoing process: a topic's subtopics have
`min_cards`/`target_cards`, a subtopic's pool can run low as users consume it, and running
low triggers a new `GenerationJob` to top it up -- coalesced per `subtopic_id` so 50
concurrent misses on the same starved slot don't spend a day of quota on one topic.

Revisiting that: a topic's curriculum already commits to a fixed card budget (~750
cards/topic, ADR-0007) and a quiz question bank sized so a user cycles through many
sessions before ever exhausting it (order 250-300 questions, exact number TBD) before
seeing a repeat -- and a repeat, once *everything* has been seen, is fine: it aids
retention rather than reading as staleness. That removes the reason a subtopic would ever
need topping up after its first pass. A topic's generation work has a natural end state:
curriculum planned, cards written to budget, questions written -- done, permanently, not
"until it needs refilling."

This also resolves what a `GenerationJob` actually represents. A topic only ever reaches
the pipeline in the first place because [ADR-0025](/work/spoin#adr-0025)'s
matching step decided it is genuinely new (not an alias onto something existing) -- so
"generate this topic" is inherently a one-time event per topic, never a recurring one.

## Decision

**A topic's generation is one pipeline run, start to finish: curriculum, then cards
(with difficulty tiers building on each other's actual content where linked), then
questions. Once that run completes, the topic is done -- no future job ever revisits it.**

```
topic arrives (post ADR-0025 matching: genuinely new)
  |
  v
curriculum call            unchanged from ADR-0007: one call, all tiers, subtopics
  |                         with target_cards, tiers linked via subtopic_group_id
  v
card generation, per subtopic, per difficulty tier
  - existing behavior unchanged: every batch sees every existing title (this
    subtopic, every difficulty) to prevent duplicates
  - NEW: for a subtopic_group's linked tiers, a higher tier's card generation
    additionally receives the ACTUAL CONTENT (not just titles) of that lower
    tier's cards, so advanced cards can genuinely build on what beginner/
    intermediate already covered rather than merely avoid repeating its titles
  |
  | cards persist and go live in the feed as soon as their subtopic/tier's
  | batch completes -- NOT held back until the whole topic (including
  | questions) finishes. Card serving and question generation proceed
  | concurrently, not sequentially, once cards for a tier exist.
  v
question generation, per subtopic, per difficulty
  - NEW: the pipeline's missing questions node (ContentGenerator.generate_questions
    already exists in the interface, unused until now) is wired into the graph
  - questions are generated FROM the cards just written for that
    subtopic/difficulty, same as content-model.md already specifies
  |
  v
topic marked done. No GenerationJob is ever created for this topic_id again.
```

### Difficulty count matters more than token count

Cost on the free tier is metered in **requests**, not tokens (ADR-0005). Passing a lower
tier's full card content into a higher tier's generation call costs nothing extra in
request count -- it's more data in the same call. The design lever here is exactly the one
ADR-0005 already established: batch more into each call rather than make more calls.

### Cross-topic parallelism and failure isolation move to the worker

Previously, `run_generation_pipeline` accepted a list of topics and the graph's own
internal `Send` fan-out ran them concurrently, sharing one DB session across the whole
call. That means one unhandled exception anywhere in the run aborts the entire batch --
acceptable when the pipeline's only caller was a manual CLI run, not acceptable once the
worker is claiming several unrelated topics' jobs per pass and a bug in one topic's
generation shouldn't take four others down with it.

**The worker now fires one `asyncio` task per claimed job, each with its own DB session,
gathered with per-task exception handling.** `run_generation_pipeline` itself is
unchanged and still accepts a topic list (the CLI can still hand it several topics at
once for convenience -- that path doesn't need isolation the way unattended worker runs
do); the worker just always calls it with a single-topic list, once per job, concurrently
across jobs.

This does not reduce what LangGraph is doing -- it clarifies the boundary ADR-0024 already
drew. LangGraph owns concurrency **within** one topic's run (subtopics and difficulty
tiers still fan out and merge inside the graph, now with a real sequencing constraint: a
linked higher tier can't start until its lower-tier sibling's cards exist). Concurrency
**across** topics/jobs is the worker's job, using plain `asyncio` -- no different in kind
from what ADR-0024's "Alternatives considered" already concluded about the worker/graph
split, just now stated for the multi-topic case specifically.

### `GenerationJob` simplifies

- `kind` (`curriculum` | `cards` | `questions`) stops meaning anything -- a job is just
  "run the one-shot pipeline for this topic," never a partial slice of it. The pipeline
  itself decides what a topic still needs (nothing does today, since a job only exists
  for a brand-new topic).
- The `subtopic_id` coalescing lock (ADR-0007's amendment to ADR-0006) is no longer
  needed -- there is no recurring per-subtopic refill to coalesce. The job's natural key
  becomes `topic_id`.
- `status`/`attempts`/`last_error`/`completed_at` are unchanged and still do real work:
  a topic's one-shot run can still fail partway (quota exhaustion, a malformed batch) and
  needs retry bookkeeping -- "one-shot" describes the *target* outcome, not a guarantee
  every attempt succeeds on the first try.

Schema migration (dropping `kind`, changing the coalescing index) is implementation work
for whoever picks up the updated task 0008 -- not decided further here beyond "the fields
described above stop being load-bearing."

## Open question: what happens to ADR-0006's feed-serving behavior?

ADR-0006 bundled two things together: (1) triggering a generation fill when a slot runs
low, and (2) how the **feed** serves a starved slot in the meantime (shorter pages,
degraded mode, hysteresis, "more coming soon" copy). This ADR only resolves (1) for
*generation* -- a topic's own initial run isn't instant, so there is still a real window
between "topic accepted" and "cards for tier X exist" where the feed has nothing to serve
for that topic. Whether that window still needs ADR-0006's degraded-mode machinery (and
whether `POOL_LOW`/`POOL_HIGH` still mean anything once there's no ongoing refill to
threshold against) is a feed-serving/read-path question this ADR deliberately leaves open
rather than deciding as a side effect of a generation-side change. `content-model.md`'s
"When the pool cannot satisfy the mix" section is flagged accordingly.

**Update (2026-08-23):** the discoverability half of this question — when a brand-new
topic starts showing up for users who didn't request it — is resolved by
[ADR-0053](/work/spoin#adr-0053). The degraded-mode/`POOL_LOW`/`POOL_HIGH`
half, for a *follower's* feed while a topic is still filling in, remains open.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- `GenerationJob` becomes simple: create one row per genuinely-new topic, run it once,
  done. No coalescing lock to reason about, no starvation detection to build.
- No recurring background cost per topic -- the budget is spent once, up front, and never
  revisited, which is easier to reason about against a hard daily quota.
- The pipeline's output is complete (cards **and** questions) the first time a topic
  finishes, rather than quizzes waiting on a separately-triggered question-generation
  path that doesn't exist yet.
- Failure isolation across jobs in one worker pass, without adding any new orchestration
  dependency -- plain `asyncio`, same tool already used for intra-pipeline concurrency.

**Harder**

- The card budget (~750/topic) and question count (~250-300, TBD) have to be genuinely
  large enough that "eventual repeat is fine" holds in practice -- get this wrong and a
  heavily-engaged user exhausts a topic and starts repeating sooner than intended, with no
  refill mechanism to fall back on anymore.
- Linked-tier content-passing needs a real answer for *how much* lower-tier content a
  higher-tier call receives -- a subtopic can have up to 25 cards per tier; passing all of
  them into every higher-tier call is more data per call every time, and needs a concrete
  design (full bodies vs summaries vs a subset) before this is implemented.
- The feed-serving open question above is genuinely unresolved and blocks nothing here,
  but does mean ADR-0006 is now partially stale in a way this ADR doesn't fully clean up.
- `GenerationJob`'s schema needs a migration (drop `kind`'s meaning, change the coalescing
  key) -- not just new code.

**Committed to**

- A topic's pipeline run produces cards **and** questions before it's considered done --
  a topic is never left with cards but no quiz bank.
- Cards go live in the feed as soon as their own subtopic/tier's batch completes, not
  gated on the whole topic (including questions) finishing.
- No `GenerationJob` is ever created for a topic that already has one completed -- one-shot
  means one-shot.
- The worker isolates failures per job (own session, own exception handling); one job's
  failure never silently marks or blocks unrelated jobs in the same pass.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep demand-driven refill, just also add questions.** Rejected: the whole reason to
drop refill is that the fixed budget (cards + questions) is now believed sufficient for
the product's actual usage pattern (repeat-after-exhaustion is acceptable), which makes
the refill machinery pure overhead with nothing left for it to react to.

**Batch the whole worker pass into one `run_generation_pipeline` call (keep the graph's
own multi-topic fan-out for cross-job concurrency), accept coarse failure attribution.**
Considered and rejected in favor of worker-level isolation -- see the reasoning above and
in the earlier discussion this ADR is written from: a batch where one topic's exception
fails four unrelated topics' jobs is a worse default than the small overhead of one
DB session per concurrent task.

**Thread lower-tier content into higher-tier prompts via a separate embedding/summary
step instead of raw content.** Not decided against, just not decided *for* -- this is the
open implementation question flagged in "Harder" above, left for whoever implements this
ADR to resolve concretely.

## Revisit when

- Measured question/card exhaustion rate for real users comes in higher than expected
  (people burn through the fixed budget faster than repeat-is-fine assumed) -- that's the
  signal to reconsider some form of top-up, not to silently widen the budget forever.
- The linked-tier content-passing design (once picked) turns out to blow up prompt size
  in practice for subtopics near the 25-card ceiling.
- The feed-serving open question above gets resolved -- this ADR should be linked from
  whatever ADR resolves it, in both directions, same as this document links back to
  ADR-0006.

adrs.title: ADR-0028: Per-key-per-model quota grid with two-pool fallback ladder
adrs.summary: Transition from a flat API key list to a 2D (key × model) quota grid with independent thinking and generator fallback ladders.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0028: Per-key-per-model quota grid, with a two-pool model fallback ladder

- **Status:** Accepted (amended by [ADR-0029](/work/spoin#adr-0029),
  [ADR-0030](/work/spoin#adr-0030), [ADR-0056](/work/spoin#adr-0056),
  [ADR-0058](/work/spoin#adr-0058))
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Resolves:** [ADR-0008](/work/spoin#adr-0008)'s open question on cloud model choice
  (the *rotation mechanism*, not the specific model ids -- those are still a first draft, see
  that ADR's updated "Open question" section)
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0074](/work/spoin#adr-0074) -- the grid is
  unchanged, but it is no longer walked per CALL. A subtopic group claims one key
  for its whole card run and walks that key's own rungs first (3.7, then 3.6, then
  -- only once no unclaimed key has room -- 3.5), and the weakest rung is held back
  as a reserve rather than being an ordinary fallback.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0029](/work/spoin#adr-0029) -- `generate_questions`
  moved from the thinking pool to the (renamed) generator pool, below. The table's
  "questions in thinking" row and its reasoning are superseded; the rest of this ADR
  (the grid mechanism, RPD/RPM split, requeue-on-exhaustion) is unchanged.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0030](/work/spoin#adr-0030) -- the thinking-pool row's
  `judge_difficulty` entry is replaced by two calls, `correct_cards` and `verify_cards`.
  Still the same pool, same "always the strongest available model" rule, and this ADR's
  grid/ladder mechanism is otherwise unaffected -- only the shape of that one call changed.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0040](/work/spoin#adr-0040) -- closes the gap this
  ADR's own "Harder" section and "Revisit when" flagged: `acquire()` grants a cell and
  returns before the actual call fires, so concurrent tasks could burst a single cell past
  its real RPM and trigger false 429s. `QuotaGovernor` now also serializes same-cell calls;
  the grid/ladder/RPD-RPM-split mechanics described below are otherwise unchanged.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0056](/work/spoin#adr-0056) -- a stalled
  call (open connection, provider never responds) now has a client-side timeout and rotates
  the same way a real 429 does, plus a background probe that checks when an excluded model
  has come back. The grid/ladder mechanism below is unchanged; this ADR adds a third kind of
  cell failure (timeout) alongside 429 and 503, and a persistent (cross-call) exclusion on
  top of the per-call one this ADR originally described.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0058](/work/spoin#adr-0058) -- this ADR treats "a real
  429" as one condition. It is two, and the provider's envelope says which: a per-MINUTE
  throttle parks a cell for a few seconds without touching the ledger, and only a per-DAY
  429 exhausts it. Conflating them made a burst of throttling read back as every key spent
  for the day. See also the correction to "it never waits" below -- the grid/ladder and
  RPD/RPM-split mechanics are otherwise unchanged.

## Context

`generation/quota.py`'s original `QuotaGovernor` rotated across `SPOIN_GEMINI_API_KEYS`
against one fixed daily target, on the assumption that each key is its own quota pool.

Checking that assumption against the actual Gemini API docs surfaced two things, both
load-bearing for how the governor needs to work:

1. **Rate limits are per Google Cloud *project*, not per API key.** Multiple keys minted
   under the same project share one pool -- rotating "keys" that all belong to one project
   buys nothing. Every entry in `SPOIN_GEMINI_API_KEYS` only helps if it is a genuinely
   separate project.
2. **Rate limits are also per *model*, independently.** Exhausting `gemini-2.5-flash`'s
   daily quota does not touch `gemini-3.5-flash`'s -- they are wholly separate buckets, on
   the same key. A rate-limit page for one project (screenshotted during this
   conversation) shows ten-plus models each with their own RPM/TPM/RPD figures.

The old governor modeled neither of these: one key = one pool, one model, one flat daily
number. It also never enforced RPM at all -- `quota_rpm` existed in `Settings` but nothing
read it.

## Decision

**The quota governor tracks a grid: `(key_index, model)` → today's spend**, not a flat list
of keys. `QuotaLedger` rows are keyed `backend=f"gemini:{key_index}:{model}"` instead of
`f"gemini:{key_index}"`.

**Two independently-rotating pools**, one `QuotaGovernor` instance each, inside
`GeminiContentGenerator`:

| Pool | Calls | Ladder |
|---|---|---|
| **thinking** | `generate_curriculum`, `match_topics`, `judge_difficulty`, `generate_questions`, `grade_free_text` | baseline Flash models, newest→oldest |
| **cards** | `generate_cards` only | "lite" Flash models, newest→oldest |

> **Superseded by [ADR-0029](/work/spoin#adr-0029):** `generate_questions`
> moved out of the thinking row into the cards row, and the pool itself was renamed
> `cards` → `generator` since it's no longer card-specific. Kept here, not edited, per this
> repo's "don't edit history" ADR rule -- read ADR-0029 for the current assignment and why.

The split follows the rule already established across this codebase (content-model.md, ADR-
0008): the thinking pool covers every call where a weak model has a real consequence -- a
bad curriculum, a bad topic match, a bad judgment, a bad quiz question, a bad grade. Card
writing is pure prose, independently checked by the quality gate afterward, so it gets the
cheap high-volume ladder instead of competing with the thinking pool's budget.

**Search order: model first, then key, and it never waits.** For a call in a pool, walk the
ladder top-down (strongest model first); for each model, try every configured key in order.
The first `(key, model)` cell with room -- on both RPD and RPM -- is used immediately. A model
is only skipped once *every* key is exhausted for it; a key that's merely RPM-capped this
second is skipped in favor of the next key or model, never slept on. Only once the entire
grid (every key × every model in the pool) is exhausted does `acquire()` raise
`QuotaExhaustedError`.

> **Correction -- "it never waits" is no longer true, and hasn't been since e6947a6.**
> Skipping a rate-limited cell in favour of the next one is still the first move, but when
> *every* remaining cell is temporarily capped (our own RPM window, or a provider cooldown
> from a per-minute 429 -- [ADR-0058](/work/spoin#adr-0058)) while still having
> daily quota left, `acquire()` now sleeps until the earliest slot opens instead of raising.
> Raising there is what turned a few seconds of throttling into a failed run.
> `QuotaExhaustedError` is now reserved for what this paragraph's last sentence says: the
> whole grid genuinely spent for the day.

Total daily capacity for a pool is therefore *(each model's RPD) × (number of configured
keys)*, summed down the ladder -- adding a key (from a genuinely separate project) adds a
full row to the grid, not a fraction of one.

**RPD is persisted, RPM is not.** RPD has to survive across the worker's separate cron
passes within the same day, so it stays in `QuotaLedger` (Postgres). RPM only needs to
survive one worker run -- the worker is a short-lived batch pass (ADR-0003 §3), not a
persistent process -- so it lives in an in-process sliding-window dict keyed by
`(key_index, model)`, reset every run. This avoids a DB round-trip per request purely to
enforce a per-minute ceiling.

**Quota exhaustion is not job failure.** `apps/worker/__main__.py` now catches
`QuotaExhaustedError` specifically (before the generic `except Exception`) and requeues the
`GenerationJob` as `pending` rather than marking it `failed`. `run_generation_pipeline` is
already idempotent per topic (ADR-0026) -- a job that stops partway because the whole grid is
spent for the day picks up exactly where it left off once a later cron pass runs after
quota resets. Before this ADR, `quota.py`'s own docstring already claimed this was "a real,
expected outcome to degrade gracefully from" -- the graceful part was never actually wired
up at the job boundary; it is now.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- Adding a key from a new project actually multiplies capacity, predictably, instead of
  silently doing nothing if it happens to share a project with an existing key.
- Quota exhaustion mid-run no longer looks identical to a real bug in `GenerationJob.status`
  -- a `pending` job that failed for capacity reasons is distinguishable from a `failed` one
  that didn't.
- RPM is now actually enforced, closing a real gap (the setting existed, nothing read it).

**Harder**

- Two `QuotaGovernor` instances and two ladders to keep in sync with whatever the actual
  free-tier limits are on a given key -- these are hand-copied from a rate-limit page, not
  fetched from an API, so they can drift as Google changes free-tier terms.
- The RPM window is in-process only, so it does NOT protect against concurrent Python
  processes hitting the same key (e.g. a manually-run CLI script racing the cron worker) --
  only the RPD figure (DB-backed) is safe across processes. Acceptable today because nothing
  runs concurrently with the worker in practice; would need to move server-side if that
  changes.
- A job that keeps hitting `QuotaExhaustedError` every cron pass (because the day's quota is
  genuinely gone) churns: requeued, reclaimed 15 minutes later, exhausted again, requeued
  again -- wasted claim-and-fail cycles until quota actually resets at midnight PT. No backoff
  is implemented; deferred as a minor inefficiency, not a correctness problem.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep one flat daily number per key, ignore the per-model reality.** Simplest, but
undercounts real capacity badly -- a key genuinely has ~5 independent 20/day buckets across
Flash variants, not one shared 20/day number, so this alternative would exhaust "quota" and
sit idle while 4/5 of the real budget went untouched.

**Block/sleep when the top choice is rate-limited, instead of falling through the grid.**
Rejected: there is almost always another `(key, model)` cell with room; sleeping wastes wall
clock the worker doesn't have much of (a 15-minute cron slice) when a fallback is sitting
right there.

**Persist RPM to Postgres like RPD.** Rejected for now: adds a DB write to every single call
purely to enforce a per-minute ceiling that only matters within one short-lived worker
process anyway. Revisit if a second concurrent process starts sharing a key (see Harder,
above).

## Revisit when

- A second process (a manual CLI run, a second worker) needs to share a key concurrently
  with the cron worker -- the in-process-only RPM window stops being safe at that point.
- The hand-copied ladder figures drift from what a key's project actually allows (a 429 from
  a cell this grid believes has room is the signal).
- The requeue-churn cost (see Harder) becomes worth fixing with an actual backoff /
  "don't reclaim before tomorrow" signal on the job row.

adrs.title: ADR-0029: Questions join generator pool
adrs.summary: Moving question generation from the constrained thinking pool to the high-throughput generator pool.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0029: Question generation moves to the generator (formerly "cards") pool

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amends:** [ADR-0028](/work/spoin#adr-0028) -- `generate_questions` moves from
  the thinking pool to the (renamed) generator pool; [ADR-0009](/work/spoin#adr-0009)
  -- retracts "questions are generated by the strongest available model, cloud only"

## Context

ADR-0028 put `generate_questions` in the thinking pool alongside curriculum, topic
matching, and judging, following ADR-0009's explicit claim that question generation
should always use the strongest available model -- a wrong answer key was judged worse
than a wrong card, since it tells a correct user they're wrong.

Revisited here: question generation is **volume work**, not judgment work. One question
per card means the same request count as card generation itself, and content-model.md's
own curriculum budget (~750 cards/topic) implies a comparably large number of questions.
Routing that volume through the thinking pool's small ladder (20 requests/day per model in
the current default) would exhaust it almost immediately on card-writing-scale traffic,
starving the calls that pool actually exists to protect (curriculum, judging, grading).

Worth noting for the record: ADR-0009's stated mitigation -- "answer keys are verified
against their source card by the batch judge" -- was never actually built. Per
`generation-pipeline.md`'s "What's missing," the quality gate is structural-only today;
nothing judges cards OR questions yet. So this decision isn't trading away a real safety
net for volume -- that net doesn't exist regardless of which model tier writes the
question. It's an argument for building the judge pass eventually, not a reason to keep
paying the thinking pool's price today for a guarantee that isn't there.

## Decision

**`generate_questions` moves to the same pool as `generate_cards`.** Both are high-volume,
one-per-item, taste-shaped prose calls (ADR-0008's "trusted for taste, never for
constraints" -- the same rule that puts card *writing* on the cheap ladder already applies
to question writing, just as directly).

**The pool is renamed `cards` → `generator`**, since it's no longer card-writing
specifically -- `SPOIN_GEMINI_CARDS_LADDER` → `SPOIN_GEMINI_GENERATOR_LADDER`,
`GeminiContentGenerator._cards`/`_cards_client()` → `_generator`/`_generator_client()`.

The thinking pool is now exactly: curriculum, topic matching, difficulty/factual judging,
quiz grading -- the calls that are either singular (one curriculum call per topic) or
directly authorization-shaped (grading a user's quiz answer), never the bulk per-item
writing calls.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- The generator pool's much larger daily budget (500/rung vs. 20/rung on current defaults)
  now covers the traffic shape it actually needs to -- cards and questions both scale with
  corpus size, and both were competing with each other's true peers (curriculum/judging
  calls, which don't scale with corpus size) under the old assignment.
- Naming now matches behavior: a pool called "cards" that also silently carried questions
  was a trap for the next person reading `langchain_impl.py`.

**Harder**

- Quiz answer keys are now written by a strictly weaker model tier than curriculum/judging,
  with no independent verification (see Context -- that verification was never built
  either way, but the gap is now paired with a weaker writer, which is a real quality risk
  worth tracking once the judge pass exists).
- `QuestionKind`'s `gen_meta.backend` recording (already present, per-question) is what
  makes this measurable after the fact -- if question quality (rejection rate, user-reported
  wrong answer keys) diverges from card quality, that's the signal in Revisit when, below.

## Alternatives considered

**Give questions their own third pool.** More precise (its own ladder, own quota grid), but
a third grid to configure and reason about for a call that behaviorally IS card generation
in every way that matters here (volume, taste-only, per-item). Not worth the extra
configuration surface until questions' quota needs actually diverge from cards'.

**Keep questions in the thinking pool, just raise its RPD.** Rejected: that widens the
thinking pool's budget for EVERY call in it, including curriculum and grading, which don't
need or want that much traffic -- it would just make the thinking pool's ladder harder to
reason about as a "small, protected budget for judgment calls."

## Revisit when

- The quality gate's judge pass (ADR-0008/0009, still unbuilt) lands and can independently
  verify answer keys -- at that point, re-evaluate whether the generator pool's weaker
  models are still an acceptable tradeoff now that there IS a safety net, versus when
  there wasn't one either way (today).
- `gen_meta`-tagged rejection or dispute rates show questions genuinely need a stronger
  model than card prose does.

adrs.title: ADR-0030: Two-pass, self-correcting quality gate
adrs.summary: Replacing discard-only validation with Pass 1 in-place topic/factual correction, local dedup, and Pass 2 difficulty verification.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0030: Two-pass, self-correcting quality gate

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0090](/work/spoin#adr-0090) — this ADR's two
  passes no longer run on the same model ladder. `verify_cards` returns a verdict and
  stays on the thinking cells permanently; `correct_cards` rewrites prose against
  retrieved source ([ADR-0089](/work/spoin#adr-0089)) and moved to the
  generator ladder, from the first pass onward. The gate is still two passes; they are
  no longer the same kind of work.
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Extended by:** [ADR-0031](/work/spoin#adr-0031) --
  adds a second feedback channel (verification rejection reasons, alongside this ADR's
  near-duplicate `avoid_bodies`) and replaces `gate_and_persist`'s four global phase-barriers
  with a per-subtopic-tier pipeline.
- **Supersedes:** [content-model.md](/work/spoin#arch-content-model)'s original "Quality
  gate" section -- checks 2-4 (topic conformance, difficulty, factual accuracy) as
  independent reject-only checks are replaced by the two-pass design below. Check 1
  (near-duplicate detection) is unchanged.
- **Amends:** [ADR-0028](/work/spoin#adr-0028) / [ADR-0008](/work/spoin#adr-0008) --
  the thinking-pool call originally specified as `judge_difficulty` (rate-and-reject, single
  pass) is replaced by two thinking-pool calls, `correct_cards` and `verify_cards`. Still the
  same pool, same "always the strongest available model" rule -- only the shape of the call
  changes.

## Context

The design content-model.md originally specified was **detect-and-reject**: an independent
LLM judge rates each card's difficulty and factual soundness in one pass, without seeing the
requested difficulty, and any disagreement fails the card. Combined with a separate,
embedding-based topic-conformance check, a card had four ways to be thrown away entire:
near-duplicate, topic drift, difficulty mismatch, factual error.

That design throws away the whole card -- and the quota already spent generating it -- for
problems that are often small and mechanically fixable: a card that's 90% on-topic but
drifted in its last paragraph, or gets one date wrong, doesn't need to be regenerated from
scratch. It needs one paragraph rewritten. Under ADR-0003's free-tier-first constraint, quota
is the scarcest resource in the system; discarding an otherwise-good card is strictly more
expensive than fixing it, when the fix costs the same one LLM call either way.

The alternative raised in review: trust the judge model to *fix* what it can, and only reject
what it genuinely can't. This ADR adopts that.

## Decision

**The gate becomes two passes over the same batch, both against the thinking pool -- never
the generator pool, regardless of which pool actually wrote the card (ADR-0008's rule:
judgment always gets the strongest available model).** Pass 1 (`correct_cards`) batches
`judge_batch_size` (20) -- it rewrites whole bodies, so its output scales with the chunk
and a big one risks the output-token cap. Pass 2 (`verify_cards`) batches
`verification_batch_size` (40) -- a verdict is a few tokens per card, so the larger chunk
is safe and halves the thinking-pool calls this pass costs per tier (the scarce rung).

### Pass 1 -- correction

The model is shown each draft's full content (`title`, `canonical_title`, `summary`, `body`)
and the **canonical topic** it must belong to (`topic.canonical_name` + `topic.description`)
-- never the loose topic phrasing that might appear inside the card's own text.
**Difficulty is withheld.**

The model may rewrite `title`/`canonical_title`/`summary`/`body` in place to make the card
actually earn its topic assignment and to fix any factual error it finds -- it never changes
*which* topic or subtopic the card belongs to, only the content underneath that assignment.
This pass always returns a result for every input card; it never rejects. If nothing needed
fixing, the returned fields are the input, unchanged.

This replaces the standalone embedding-based topic-conformance check from content-model.md:
topic fit becomes something the model actively repairs, not something a cosine threshold
merely flags for disposal.

`content_embedding` is (re)computed from **pass 1's corrected `body`**, never the
pre-correction draft -- every downstream comparison (dedup, and eventually ranking) has to
read the text that actually shipped.

### Near-duplicate detection -- unchanged, runs here

Content-model.md's check 1 is untouched: local, free (`fastembed`/`HashEmbedder`, hard rule
5), subtopic-scoped against the existing corpus, plus an intra-batch comparison (the
same-batch problem ADR-0007 already named -- a model can write near-identical cards within
one response, and neither the corpus comparison nor the curriculum's title-list prevention
catches that).

**Intra-batch comparison is a running set.** Each new card (post pass-1 correction) is
compared only against cards already *accepted* earlier in the same batch, in order -- not an
all-pairs comparison. This mirrors how the corpus comparison already works (compare against
what exists so far) and keeps the cost linear in batch size.

A hit here -- corpus or intra-batch, above `card_duplicate_threshold` -- is a **hard reject**,
and happens **before** pass 2. There's no reason to spend a second LLM call verifying a card
that's about to be thrown out for being a duplicate of something else.

### Pass 2 -- verification

Survivors of dedup go back to the model, batched the same way, now **with their requested
difficulty visible**. The model:

- Confirms (or, if it disagrees, states) the difficulty the corrected content actually reads
  as.
- Gives a final `accepted: bool` -- catching anything pass 1's edit didn't actually resolve.

`accepted = false` here is a real, final rejection -- unlike pass 1, which never rejects.

### Rejections are persisted, not discarded

A card that fails structural validation, near-dup, or pass 2 verification is written to a new
`rejected_card` table (topic/subtopic, requested difficulty, the corrected title/body at time
of rejection, `stage` -- `structural` | `near_duplicate` | `verification` -- a `reason` string,
and `gen_meta`) instead of vanishing. It never becomes a `Card` row and is never counted
toward a subtopic's `existing_count`, so the next generation run (or a same-run top-up, if one
is ever added) sees the subtopic as still under target and fills the gap naturally.

The reasoning: content-model.md already treats a rejected card as informative (`gen_meta`
lets a bad *batch* be traced), and a per-card labeled example -- draft plus the specific reason
it failed -- is strictly more useful than a log line, for future work like evaluating gate
accuracy or fine-tuning the generator. Discarding it for free throws that away for nothing.

### Difficulty calibration examples

`difficulty` is a label; without a concrete anchor for what "beginner" versus "advanced"
actually *reads like*, both the writer (`generate_cards`) and the judge (`correct_cards`/
`verify_cards`) are calibrating against nothing but the word itself. Both now accept a
`difficulty_examples: dict[Difficulty, list[str]]` -- a few example card bodies per tier,
shown together so the *contrast* between tiers is visible, not just one tier in isolation.

**Source depends on whether the subtopic-tier is linked or standalone:**

- **Linked** (multiple tiers share a `subtopic_group_id` -- `SubtopicGroupPlan.tiers` has more
  than one entry): no separate examples are needed. `builds_on` (ADR-0026) already gives the
  higher tier the actual lower-tier cards for this exact concept, which is a more relevant,
  concept-specific calibration than a generic example could be. `difficulty_examples` is
  passed empty here.
- **Standalone** (`SubtopicGroupPlan.tiers` has exactly one entry -- the common case, since
  curricula are never forced to give a concept all three tiers): there is nothing in-subtopic
  to draw from, so a **hand-curated, topic-agnostic example catalog** fills the gap -- same
  "schema/plumbing now, content later" pattern as ADR-0021's ASCII scene catalog.
  `content/difficulty_examples.py` exists and is wired into every call site; the catalog
  itself is empty (returns `[]` per tier) until authored -- see
  [docs/tasks/0011](../tasks/0011-difficulty-example-catalog.md).

The judge's pass 1 (correction) receives the same three-tier example set regardless of which
specific difficulty a given card was requested at -- showing all three together doesn't leak
which one applies to *this* card, since every card in the batch sees the identical set. Pass 2
(verification) receives it too, now alongside the visible requested difficulty, for the same
calibration reason.

### Duplicate-content feedback loop

A near-duplicate rejection is wasted quota unless something changes before the same
subtopic-tier is asked to generate again. `_load_subtopic_plans` (pipeline.py) now also
fetches this exact subtopic-tier's most recent `rejected_card` rows with
`stage = near_duplicate` (capped at `settings.max_duplicate_feedback_bodies`, newest first)
and threads their **full body text** into the next `generate_cards` call as `avoid_bodies` --
distinct from `existing_titles` (titles of cards that were *accepted*): this is the actual
rejected content, shown as "do not write anything like this again," because duplication is a
body-similarity phenomenon a title alone can't convey.

Scoped to the exact subtopic (not the group) -- matching where the near-dup check itself is
scoped (`generation/dedup.py`'s corpus comparison), not the group-wide scope `existing_titles`
uses for cross-tier depth differentiation.

**This closes the loop only across separate pipeline runs, not within one run's retry
rounds.** `generate_subtopic_cards`' multi-round top-up loop (same node, same call) has no DB
access by design -- near-duplicate detection only happens later, once, in `gate_and_persist`,
so a rejection discovered there can't inform a round that already ran earlier in the same
`run_generation_pipeline` call. It DOES inform the next time generation runs for that
subtopic -- a later top-up pass, or a manual re-trigger -- which is the common case for an
under-target subtopic (ADR-0026's one-shot model means a shortfall gets revisited later, not
retried in a tight loop within the same call).

### Everything runs on every card

Same principle as content-model.md originally stated for the judge: batching makes this
affordable on the whole corpus, not a sample. Pass 1, dedup, and pass 2 all run on every
draft that survives the previous step -- no check in this gate is sampled.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- Fewer good cards thrown away for a fixable problem -- the common case (a mostly-right card
  with one wrong detail) now costs one LLM call to fix rather than one LLM call to discard
  plus another to regenerate.
- One coherent two-step "gate" replaces four independently-reasoned checks; topic conformance
  no longer needs its own embedding comparison and threshold to calibrate.
- Rejected drafts become a queryable, labeled dataset instead of a discarded batch -- useful
  later for evaluating the gate itself or the generator.

**Harder**

- **Doubles the thinking-pool cost of gating.** What was designed as one call per batch of 20
  (content-model.md's original judge) is now two -- pass 1 and pass 2 both hit the thinking
  pool's much smaller ladder (ADR-0028/0029), on top of curriculum, topic matching, and
  grading already sharing it.
- **Pass 1 can silently rewrite a card in ways nobody downstream sees.** There is no separate
  detector watching the corrector the way there was a standalone topic-conformance check --
  pass 2's spot-check (difficulty + final accept/reject) is the only backstop, and it isn't
  designed to catch "technically on-topic but now bland/generic" drift from over-correction.
- A card that fails pass 2 (e.g. a genuine difficulty disagreement) is discarded even though
  pass 1 already spent a rewrite on it -- `rejected_card` makes that sunk cost auditable, not
  avoided.
- `card_duplicate_threshold` remains uncalibrated (see content-model.md's open questions,
  and the note below) -- this ADR doesn't resolve that, it only fixes where in the pipeline
  the check runs.

**Committed to**

- Every draft that reaches the gate becomes exactly one of: an `active` `Card` row, or a
  `rejected_card` row. Nothing is silently dropped.
- `content_embedding` always reflects post-pass-1-correction body text.
- Both passes always run on the thinking pool, never the generator pool, regardless of which
  backend (cloud/local) wrote the original draft.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the original four-independent-check, reject-only design.** Rejected per Context: wastes
the fixable-card case, which is the common case, not the exception.

**Fold near-duplicate detection into the LLM passes too** (tell the model "don't repeat
this list"). Rejected: this is exactly the weak negative-constraint problem ADR-0007 already
rejected for curriculum title lists -- LLMs are unreliable at avoiding a list, and cosine
similarity against the actual corpus is precise, free, and already built. Keep it as its own
step.

**Single verification-only pass, no correction pass** (i.e., actually wire up `judge_difficulty`
as originally speced, unchanged). Rejected in this conversation -- see Context: it's strictly
worse on quota for the common fixable-card case, for no accuracy benefit pass 2 alone
wouldn't already provide.

**Merge pass 1 and pass 2 into one call** (show difficulty from the start, ask for
correct-and-verify in one shot). Considered and rejected for now: asking a model to both edit
content AND independently critique whether that content matches a difficulty it was shown
risks the same self-report problem `DifficultyVerdict` was built to avoid in the first place --
seeing its own edit next to the answer makes "does this match?" too easy to rubber-stamp.
Keeping difficulty hidden until after the edit is committed is what makes pass 2 a genuine
independent check rather than the model grading its own homework in the same breath.

## Revisit when

- Real rejection/edit-rate data exists: if pass 1's edit rate is high enough that corrected
  cards start reading like a different voice than the generator's, the correction pass may
  need its own spot-check, not just pass 2's.
- The doubled thinking-pool cost (see Harder) becomes the actual bottleneck against ADR-0028's
  ladder -- at that point, consider skipping pass 1 for cards a cheap heuristic already thinks
  are fine, or merging the passes per the rejected alternative above once there's a cheaper way
  to avoid the self-grading risk.
- `card_duplicate_threshold` gets real calibration data from `fastembed` (task 0001-adjacent
  follow-up) -- see content-model.md's open questions; this ADR ships it at `0.9` as an explicit,
  more-conservative-than-0.93 placeholder pending that.

adrs.title: ADR-0031: Verification feedback and per-tier gate durability
adrs.summary: Threading rejection feedback into subsequent generation runs and making gating durable at the subtopic-tier level.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0031: Verification rejection feedback, and a per-tier durable gate

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-17
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amends:** [ADR-0030](/work/spoin#adr-0030) -- extends its "Duplicate-content
  feedback loop" section with a second feedback channel, and replaces `gate_and_persist`'s
  four global phase-barriers with a per-subtopic-tier pipeline.

## Context

Two gaps showed up running the pipeline against real Gemini keys across a full topic:
