1. **Pass-2 verification rejections were dead ends.** ADR-0030 already closes the loop for
   near-duplicate rejections (`avoid_bodies` -- full body text, no reasoning, since a
   similarity score is all dedup has). Verification rejections carry something dedup
   doesn't: a real `reason` string the judge model gave (e.g. "reads as intermediate, not
   advanced"). That reason was persisted to `rejected_card` and then never read again -- the
   next run's writer had no way to know a subtopic-tier had failed verification before, let
   alone why.
2. **`gate_and_persist` was four global barriers over the whole batch** (correct everything,
   dedup everything, verify everything, persist everything, generate all questions) sharing
   one uncommitted session until the very end. A crash or quota exhaustion partway through a
   large multi-subtopic batch discarded every tier's already-spent LLM calls, not just the
   one in flight. Separately, a subtopic-tier that already had its cards but was interrupted
   before its questions were written (cards and questions commit as conceptually separate
   steps) had no path back -- `existing_count` meeting `target_cards` makes
   `generate_subtopic_cards` skip drafting new cards for that tier on every future run,
   so nothing ever revisited it to backfill the missing questions.

## Decision

**Verification feedback loop.** `_load_subtopic_plans` fetches this exact subtopic-tier's
most recent `rejected_card` rows with `stage = VERIFICATION` (capped at
`settings.max_verification_feedback_bodies`, newest first, same recency-capped shape as
`avoid_duplicate_bodies`) as `(body, reason)` pairs, threaded into the next `generate_cards`
call as `rejection_feedback`. The prompt shows both, with the reason framed as the actual
problem to fix -- distinct from `avoid_bodies`, which has no reasoning to show.

**Curriculum commits as soon as it's planned.** `resolve_and_plan_topic` commits right after
setting `topic.curriculum_generated_at`, instead of leaving it pending until
`gate_and_persist`'s fan-in. Card generation that follows does no DB access at all, so this
was free durability being left on the table.

**Missing-question backfill.** `_load_subtopic_plans` also fetches this subtopic's active
cards with no `Question` row (an outer join against `Question`). `generate_subtopic_cards`
threads these through unconditionally -- including on the early-return path where a tier is
already at target and drafts nothing new -- as `cards_missing_questions`.

**Per-tier gate, not global phases.** `_process_gate_item` runs one subtopic-tier's entire
trip through the gate -- correction, dedup, verification, persist, question generation
(now over newly-accepted cards plus any backfilled `cards_missing_questions`) -- start to
finish, independent of every sibling tier. Every tier runs via `asyncio.gather`. The LLM
phases touch no DB and run fully concurrently under the existing semaphore; dedup and
persist do touch `runtime.session`, which is not safe for concurrent use across coroutines,
so those sections serialize through a new `session_lock` instead of being pulled out into a
separate global phase. Each tier commits as soon as its own cards (and then its questions)
are written, not at one shared end-of-batch commit.

### Addendum 2026-08-18: backfill-aware question prompts

Two gaps showed up once the missing-question backfill above was live-tested against real
Gemini keys across several reruns:

1. **The writer had no idea a call was a backfill.** `_generate_questions_for_group` already
   combined newly-drafted cards and `cards_missing_questions` backfill cards into one
   undifferentiated list before this addendum, so `generate_questions` prompted the model as
   if every card were brand-new, unproven content -- even for a card that had already cleared
   the full gate in an earlier run and simply lost its question to an interrupted or failed
   prior call.
2. **The writer had no visibility into a subtopic-tier's existing questions.** Nothing told
   the model what quiz angles this subtopic already covers, so a backfill or a later
   generation round could plausibly repeat a question already asked (in spirit if not
   verbatim) -- the same blind-spot `existing_titles` already solves for card generation, just
   never extended to questions.

`_process_gate_item` now calls `_generate_questions_for_group` (and, underneath it,
`ContentGenerator.generate_questions`) up to twice per subtopic-tier, never mixing the two
cases in one call: once for cards drafted THIS run (`is_backfill=False`), once for
`cards_missing_questions` backfill cards (`is_backfill=True`). Both calls receive
`existing_stems` -- this subtopic-tier's already-active question stems, capped at
`settings.max_existing_question_stems` (loaded once in `_load_subtopic_plans`, same query
shape as every other feedback list this ADR and ADR-0030 already load there) -- and the SECOND
call's `existing_stems` additionally includes whatever the FIRST call just wrote, so a
two-call tier doesn't duplicate against itself within the same run, not just against prior
runs.

`_QUESTIONS_SYSTEM` explains what `[BACKFILL]`-tagged cards mean (already accepted, simply
missing a question -- write with full confidence, don't hedge or re-review) and instructs the
model not to repeat any stem shown in the existing-questions block.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- A subtopic-tier that fails verification repeatedly now gets progressively better feedback
  instead of retrying blind -- closes the same class of wasted-quota loop ADR-0030 already
  fixed for near-duplicates, for the other rejection stage that has real reasoning to offer.
- A crash, quota exhaustion, or process kill mid-batch now only loses the tiers still in
  flight. Previously-committed tiers (and the curriculum) stay committed regardless of what
  happens to the rest of the run.
- A subtopic stuck with cards but no questions (an interrupted prior run) self-heals on the
  next `generate_topics` invocation instead of staying broken forever.

**Harder**

- `gate_and_persist` now issues many small commits instead of one batch commit -- more round
  trips to the DB, though each is small (one tier's cards, then that tier's questions).
- `session_lock` means dedup/persist across tiers is still effectively sequential relative to
  each other (only the LLM phases actually run concurrent within a tier's own pipeline) --
  this trades some theoretical DB-write parallelism for correctness, since `AsyncSession`
  can't be shared across concurrent coroutines at all.
- `rejection_feedback` and `avoid_bodies` are now both threaded into the same prompt; at
  high rejection volume for one subtopic-tier this grows the prompt by two feedback blocks
  instead of one -- bounded by their respective `max_*_feedback_bodies` settings, same
  mitigation ADR-0030 already relies on for `avoid_bodies`.

**Committed to**

- Every subtopic-tier's gate outcome (cards persisted, questions persisted) is now visible
  and durable independently of every other tier in the same batch.
- A tier with cards but no questions is a recoverable, self-healing state, not a permanent
  gap requiring manual intervention.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep one global commit at the end of `gate_and_persist`, only add the curriculum
mid-commit.** Rejected: the whole point of the per-tier crash observed in practice was
losing already-gated cards from *earlier* tiers in the same batch, not just the curriculum.

**Backfill missing questions as a separate maintenance script/cron job instead of inline in
the normal generation path.** Rejected: `_load_subtopic_plans` already visits every
subtopic on every `generate_topics` call; a separate job would duplicate that traversal and
add another thing to remember to run, for a case (interrupted prior run) that's naturally
caught by the existing entry point.

**Fold `rejection_feedback` and `avoid_bodies` into one combined list instead of two
prompt-visible sections.** Rejected: they mean different things to the writer (near-dup says
"don't write this again"; verification feedback says "here's specifically what was wrong") --
collapsing them would lose the reason string's specificity inside undifferentiated body text.

## Revisit when

- Real second-pass data exists on whether `rejection_feedback` actually reduces the
  verification reject rate on a retry -- this ships ADR-0030-shaped but untested against real
  content beyond unit tests of prompt threading.
- The per-tier commit granularity shows up as a real DB round-trip cost at scale (many
  subtopic-tiers, small batches) -- at that point, consider batching commits across a few
  tiers rather than one-per-tier, trading back some crash-blast-radius for fewer round trips.

adrs.title: ADR-0040: Serialize actual network calls per (key, model) cell
adrs.summary: Eliminating false 429 burst errors by locking same-cell network invocations while preserving full concurrency across independent grid cells.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0040: Serialize actual network calls per (key, model) cell

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-19
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Reframed by:** [ADR-0074](/work/spoin#adr-0074) -- NOT superseded.
  One key per subtopic group makes same-cell contention rare, so `cell_lock` is
  usually uncontended; it is still required for the multi-tier gate fan-out and for
  two processes reaching the same cell. Do not delete it as "no longer needed".
  That ADR also keeps this one's `note_request_sent` send-time re-stamp explicitly.
- **Revisit condition met from:** [ADR-0028](/work/spoin#adr-0028) — "A second
  process... needs to share a key concurrently" was the anticipated trigger; what actually
  hit was concurrency *within* one process, a gap that ADR didn't cover.

## Context

Running `generate_topics` for two topics (and later for one topic alone) produced real 429s
from the Gemini API on cells the local `QuotaLedger` believed had room — the exact drift
ADR-0028 flagged as a live risk, but happening far more than expected: dozens of cells,
seconds apart, well under both the configured RPD and RPM ceilings.

The cause was a gap in `QuotaGovernor.acquire()`'s contract: it grants a `(key, model)` cell
and records the RPM hit immediately, then returns — the actual HTTP call happens later, made
by the caller (`langchain_impl.py`'s `_invoke_with_retry`). Nothing stops several concurrently
running subtopic tasks (up to `max_concurrent_generation_calls`) from each acquiring a
*different* cell in the same instant and firing their HTTP calls together. Our sliding window
tracks *acquired* count, not *in-flight* count, so it saw "room" the whole time — the actual
burst pattern arriving at Google's own limiter is invisible to it.

Compounding this: `mark_exhausted()` treats any real 429 as proof the cell is genuinely spent
for the rest of the day, force-setting `requests_spent = rpd`. That's the right response to a
*real* exhaustion signal, but it also permanently poisons a cell that only 429'd because of
this burst pattern — one false 429 early in a run writes off a cell's entire daily budget,
even though the provider-side usage was nowhere near its real limit.

## Decision

Three approaches were tried in order before landing on the one kept:

1. **Lower the configured RPD/RPM ladder numbers below the real dashboard limits**, to leave
   headroom. Rejected on reflection — it doesn't touch the actual bug (calls still fire in a
   burst), just makes the burst smaller and harder to notice; wastes real, usable quota for
   no structural fix.
2. **Random jitter delay (0–10s) after a cell is granted, before the call fires.** An
   improvement — spreads departures across a window — but still probabilistic. Two calls to
   the same cell can still land close together by chance, and it does nothing to help
   *legitimately* concurrent calls to *different* cells finish sooner.
3. **Per-cell serialization: queue calls to the same `(key, model)` cell, one at a time,
   waiting for each to finish before the next fires.** This is the one kept. It directly
   matches the actual hazard — same-cell bursts — without touching the concurrency across
   *different* cells (independent quota, no reason to slow those down).

`QuotaGovernor` gained `cell_lock(key_index, model) -> asyncio.Lock`, one lock per cell,
created lazily. `_invoke_with_retry` holds this lock around the actual network call (not
around `acquire()`, which already has its own separate lock for the DB/window bookkeeping).
Same-cell calls now queue in FIFO order and wait for the prior call to complete; different
cells still run fully concurrently, so aggregate throughput across the grid is unaffected.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- The RPM ceiling in the ladder config now means what it says — a cell can't be driven over
  its configured rate by request bursts from this process's own concurrency.
- No more false 429s means `mark_exhausted()` fires only on genuine exhaustion, so a cell's
  daily budget isn't wasted by a race that had nothing to do with real usage.

**Harder**

- A cell that's mid-call now blocks a second task that wants the *same* cell — that task
  effectively waits out the first call's full round-trip (seen taking up to 30s+) before it
  can even attempt its own request. Acceptable: with 9 keys × several models per pool, tasks
  land on a shared cell rarely, and the alternative (bursting) was strictly worse.
- Doesn't address the existing gap ADR-0028 already named in "Harder": the RPM window and now
  the cell locks are both in-process only, so a second OS process (e.g. a manual CLI run
  racing the cron worker) still isn't protected.
- Today's `QuotaLedger` rows are already poisoned from before this fix landed — most cells
  show `requests_spent` forced to their RPD ceiling by a false 429, even though Google's own
  dashboard shows well under half of real daily quota used. That mismatch is now understood
  (see this session's ledger inspection) but not yet remedied; the poisoned rows persist until
  the day rolls over or someone resets them by hand.

## Alternatives considered

**Global single-flight queue (one call in flight across the ENTIRE grid, not per cell).**
Considered directly — simplest possible fix, guaranteed no burst. Rejected: throws away the
whole point of the multi-key grid (ADR-0028) by serializing all 9 keys' independent quota
down to the throughput of one. Per-cell locking gets the same burst-safety without that cost.

**Persist an in-flight counter to Postgres alongside RPD.** Would make the "room" check
account for calls that were granted but haven't completed yet, closing the gap more directly
than a lock. Rejected for now — same DB-round-trip-per-call cost ADR-0028 already rejected for
RPM, and the lock achieves the same practical outcome without it.

## Revisit when

- A second OS process needs to share a key concurrently with this one (still open from
  ADR-0028 — cell locks don't close it either, being in-process only).
- The poisoned ledger rows from before this fix need an actual remedy (a manual reset, or
  `mark_exhausted` softened to not force the FULL day's budget on one 429) rather than waiting
  for midnight PT rollover.

adrs.title: ADR-0041: Per-group gate and persist
adrs.summary: Persisting cards and making them live in the feed as soon as their subtopic group finishes, removing global fan-in write bottlenecks.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0041: Gate+persist per subtopic group, not after a global fan-in

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-20
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0074](/work/spoin#adr-0074) -- per-group
  gate+persist for CARDS is unchanged and still the point of this ADR. Question
  generation moves out of the per-group path to a topic-wide phase at the fan-in.
- **Fixes a drift from:** [ADR-0026](/work/spoin#adr-0026), whose own
  Decision section already states "cards persist and go live in the feed as soon as their
  subtopic/tier's batch completes" — the graph wiring never actually implemented that.

## Context

Running a two-topic generation pass and checking the DB mid-run surfaced that **zero**
cards had persisted despite dozens of subtopic-tiers having already finished drafting
(visible in the logs as "hero card --" and "round N got M card(s)" lines). Tracing the
graph (`_build_graph()`) showed why: `generate_subtopic_cards` (one branch per subtopic
group, fanned out via `Send`, across every topic in the run) fed its results into
`card_results`, a reducer-accumulated state key that only `gate_and_persist` reads — and
`gate_and_persist` is wired with a plain `add_edge`, which in LangGraph is a fan-in: it
does not run until **every** `generate_subtopic_cards` branch, across every topic and every
group, has returned.

That is a global barrier between "draft everything" and "gate+persist everything" — the
opposite of what ADR-0026 decided. Its Decision section is explicit: card serving and
question generation should proceed "as soon as cards for a tier exist," not wait on the
rest of the run. The code had drifted from the doc it was supposed to implement.

## Decision

**`generate_subtopic_cards` gates and persists its own group's cards and questions itself,
immediately, before returning** — by calling `_gate_and_persist_results` (the gate/dedup/
persist logic extracted, unchanged, from the old `gate_and_persist` body) at the end of its
own function, instead of only returning draft `CardDraft`s for someone else to process
later.

`gate_and_persist` stays in the graph as the final node, still reached via the same
fan-in edge — but by the time it runs, every card and question this run will write is
**already committed**. Its only remaining job is aggregating each group's `item_reports`
into the run's final per-topic report and marking each topic's `GenerationJob.progress`
done. Fan-in is the right shape for that specific purpose (a topic's final report and
"done" flag genuinely do need every one of its groups finished) — it was only wrong as a
gate on the actual DB writes.

`PipelineState.card_results` (raw drafts, accumulated globally) is replaced by
`item_reports` (small per-tier report dicts — accepted/rejected/failed counts, not card
content) for exactly that narrower final purpose. `SubtopicGroupPlan` gained
`topic_description`, threaded from `resolve_and_plan_topic`, since a `Send`-invoked branch
only sees its own payload (not the graph's accumulated state) and `generate_subtopic_cards`
now needs it directly to gate its own group instead of looking it up from `topic_plans`
later.

The "one writer" rule from ADR-0026/0030 is preserved in spirit: `_gate_and_persist_results`
/ `_process_gate_item` remain the *only* functions containing gate/persist logic — this
changes how many times and when that logic runs (once per group, as soon as the group is
ready), not how many places contain it.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- Cards and questions now actually appear in the DB/feed incrementally, matching what
  ADR-0026 already promised and what the live-progress UI implies is happening.
- A crash or quota exhaustion partway through a large multi-topic run now loses only the
  groups still drafting, not every group's already-gated-and-persisted work sitting behind
  a barrier that never got reached.
- Gating for one group can now overlap with drafting for another, rather than strictly
  waiting — a minor throughput win, not the primary motivation.

**Harder**

- `gate_and_persist`'s final report and "topic done" marking are now visibly decoupled from
  when a topic's cards actually became servable — a topic can be fully playable in the feed
  well before its `GenerationJob.progress` reads "done." Not a new problem (ADR-0026 already
  intended this gap to exist), but now it's real instead of theoretical, and anything reading
  `progress.stage` for a "can I serve this topic yet" decision would be wrong to do so.
- One more function (`generate_subtopic_cards`) now touches the DB and needs to reason about
  `runtime.session_lock`, where before only `gate_and_persist`'s call tree did. The lock
  itself already handles this safely (unchanged), but the "no DB access" invariant that used
  to make this function trivially safe to reason about is gone.

## Alternatives considered

**Restructure the graph so `gate_and_persist` itself is `Send`-fanned per group** (one
invocation per group, routed directly from `generate_subtopic_cards` via `Command.goto`,
instead of inlining the call). Rejected as unnecessary complexity: it would need a separate
mechanism to detect "every group of THIS topic has now gated" for the final per-topic report
and done-marking, which a plain function call from inside `generate_subtopic_cards` gets for
free by just... calling it inline and returning the report alongside everything else that
node already returns.

**Persist drafts as they're generated, per round, inside `generate_subtopic_cards`'s round
loop** (finer-grained than per-group). Rejected: the quality gate's correction/dedup/
verification passes work in batches for a real reason (ADR-0005's batching economics,
ADR-0030's calibration), and a subtopic-tier's own rounds aren't independent of each other
(later rounds see `existing_titles` from earlier ones) — per-group is the natural unit
ADR-0026 already specified ("subtopic/tier's batch"), not per-round.

## Revisit when

- `GenerationJob.progress` semantics get relied on for a "can this topic be served yet"
  decision anywhere in the read path — the note above needs to become an actual check
  against real committed card counts instead, not the job's `stage` field.
- A future change reintroduces a reason to batch gate/persist across MULTIPLE groups again
  (e.g. a quality-gate pass that benefits from seeing more than one group's cards at once) —
  would need to reopen this ADR's "per group" granularity, not silently work around it.

adrs.title: ADR-0047: Removal of legacy concurrency semaphore
adrs.summary: Removing the obsolete global asyncio.Semaphore(5) bottle-neck and delegating all rate limiting to the multi-key QuotaGovernor.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0047: Removal of Legacy Concurrency Semaphore in Generation Pipeline

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Reframed by:** [ADR-0074](/work/spoin#adr-0074) -- NOT reversed.
  That ADR does not reintroduce a global semaphore; it gives each subtopic group
  ownership of one KEY, so parallelism still scales with the key pool exactly as this
  ADR wanted. It does knowingly give back some of the utilization won here (a claimed
  key can idle), because ADR-0073 capped demand at one topic per worker pass and
  predictability became worth more than packing. The dead
  `max_concurrent_generation_calls` setting this ADR's removal left behind in
  `core/config.py` -- read by nothing since -- is deleted there.

## Context

During early development of the generation pipeline ([ADR-0024](/work/spoin#adr-0024), [ADR-0026](/work/spoin#adr-0026)), the system did not yet have a multi-key, per-model quota governor. To prevent a single API key from triggering rate limits (429s), an outer global semaphore (`runtime.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(settings.max_concurrent_generation_calls)`, default `5`) was wrapped around every generator, gate, and question generation call in `pipeline/nodes.py`.

Later, [ADR-0028](/work/spoin#adr-0028) and [ADR-0040](/work/spoin#adr-0040) introduced a complete, self-contained `QuotaGovernor`:
1. **Per-cell sliding window deques** (`_rpm_has_room`) that enforce exact per-key, per-model RPM ceilings without cross-key interference.
2. **Per-cell call serialization** (`cell_lock`) that serializes concurrent calls to the *same* key while allowing different keys to execute fully concurrently.
3. **Atomic ledger tracking** for daily quotas (RPD) with automatic multi-key fallback.

### The Problem / Testing Impact ("The 40-Key Ferrari in a School Zone")

While the subtopic fan-out in LangGraph was triumphantly made unbounded in Task 0014 / commit `d5bb804`, the forgotten `runtime.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(5)` remained quietly standing at the front door like an overzealous bouncer.

During multi-topic production test runs with a massive fleet of 40+ Gemini API keys:
- We built a 40-cylinder Ferrari capable of **>600 Requests Per Minute** with precision per-cell locks, sliding deque windows, and multi-key fallback ladders.
- Yet, this lone semaphore forced the entire 40-key fleet to merge into a single, polite 5-car single-file lane.
- **The Result**: A 3-topic curriculum generation run (176 subtopic tiers, 3,275 production cards, ~3,000 quiz questions) took an agonizing **2.8 hours (~165 minutes)** while developers watched in existential dread as the progress meter hovered at "99.9%" across chained tiers, wondering if the universe itself was rate-limiting them.
- In reality, the keys were essentially on vacation (>90% idle headroom), sipping margaritas while waiting for the semaphore to let 5 requests through at a time.


## Decision

1. **Remove `runtime.semaphore` entirely from `_Runtime`, `graph.py`, and `nodes.py`**:
   - `QuotaGovernor` is now the single source of truth for rate limiting, concurrency, and key rotation.
   - Subtopics and batches dispatch their LLM calls directly to the `QuotaGovernor`.
   - The governor's sliding deque window and per-cell locks safely govern request throughput across all available keys in parallel.

## Consequences

- **True Multi-Key Concurrency**: The pipeline can now utilize all available API keys simultaneously without being throttled by an arbitrary 5-call global ceiling.
- **Drastically Reduced Generation Time**: Multi-topic generation runs with large key pools scale throughput linearly with the number of available keys.
- **Safety Preserved**: Per-key RPM (15 RPM on Flash-Lite, 5 RPM on Flash) remains strictly enforced by `QuotaGovernor._rpm_windows` and `cell_lock`, preventing 429s.

adrs.title: ADR-0048: CockroachDB Basic over Neon, for corpus storage headroom
adrs.summary: Moving corpus storage to CockroachDB Basic ahead of Neon's 500MB free-tier ceiling, measured against real per-topic storage costs.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0048: CockroachDB Basic over Neon, for corpus storage headroom

- **Status:** Accepted (amends 0003)
- **Date:** 2026-08-22
- **Deciders:** Anubhav

## Context

ADR-0003 picked Neon's free tier and stated the binding constraint plainly: **not
storage — LLM generation quota**. That was true when it was written, and it is still
true about *generation throughput*. It stopped being true about *storage* the moment
the target corpus size changed.

The product goal is now **1,000+ topics before paying anything**, with custom user
topics on top. That is a different number than ADR-0003 was reasoning about, and it
is what makes this a storage decision rather than a preference.

### What the corpus actually costs, measured

Measured against the live `spoin_db` on 2026-08-22 (read-only, `pg_database_size` and
row counts):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Whole database | 46 MB |
| `card` / `question` tables | 21 MB / 13 MB |
| Topics with generated content | 7 (8 more exist as empty shells) |
| Cards / questions | 6,884 / 5,206 |
| **Per generated topic** | **~983 cards, ~744 questions, ~4.9 MB** |

Per-topic cost varies by roughly 3x — "Current AI Capabilities" is 476 cards, "Operating
Systems" is 1,739. So a topic costs **3–9 MB**, averaging ~5 MB.

Projected against the two ceilings:

| Corpus | Size | Neon free (500 MB) | CockroachDB Basic (10 GiB) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7 topics (today) | 46 MB | 9% | 0.4% |
| 50 topics | ~260 MB | **52%** | 2.5% |
| ~100 topics | ~500 MB | **at the ceiling** | 5% |
| 1,000 topics (avg) | ~5 GB | 10x over | 50% |
| 1,000 topics (heavy) | ~9 GB | 18x over | **90%** |

**Neon's free tier runs out at roughly 100 topics** — a tenth of the stated goal, and
only twice the near-term 50-topic plan. This is not a distant problem being solved
early; it is reachable within the current expansion.

## Decision

**Move the corpus database from Neon to CockroachDB Basic**, whose free allowance is
10 GiB of storage per organization per month (part of a $15/month credit that also
covers 50M Request Units).

ADR-0003 §2's rule — *no accommodation may require a rewrite to undo* — is honored,
not waived. Scaling past 10 GiB on CockroachDB is still a billing toggle with an
unchanged connection string. What changes is *which* free tier we sit on before that
toggle, and the migration is paid for once, now, at 46 MB, rather than later at
5 GB under load.

**This decision is gated on a spike (task 0016) proving the stack runs on CockroachDB
at all.** If the dialect, vector, or migration story fails there, the fallback is
ADR-0003's original answer: pay for Neon. Do not force this through.

> **Spike outcome (2026-08-31): GO.** Task 0016 stood a CockroachDB v26.2.6 node
> up locally, ran the suite and isolated probes against it, and returned **go**.
> The dialect connects, `VECTOR(384)`/`<=>` work natively (`pgvector.sqlalchemy.Vector`
> stays — models untouched), and the **full 23-migration Alembic chain applies
> clean base → head**, producing a schema identical to the live Postgres DB. The
> residue is scoped into tasks 0017–0019 (see 0016's hand-back for the classified
> list). Two rows of the compatibility table below were **wrong** and are corrected
> inline. The real ongoing cost is unchanged from what this ADR predicted:
> `SERIALIZABLE` + a bounded `40001` retry boundary for the request write paths
> (task 0019). The spike also found `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` can *skip a
> freshly-committed unlocked row* in the write-intent window — but the
> worker/quota claim transactions are short-lived, so the fix is just to drop
> `SKIP LOCKED` for plain `FOR UPDATE` (task 0019 step 0), not a redesign.

### What this decision is *not*

It is **not** an adoption of the event-streaming half of the proposal it came from.
Kafka is separately and explicitly rejected — see [ADR-0049](/work/spoin#adr-0049).
Storage was never a problem a message broker solves, and bundling the two would have
bought one real fix at the price of two new operational systems.

### The compatibility surface, verified rather than assumed

CockroachDB is Postgres-wire-compatible, not Postgres. What we actually depend on:

| Dependency | Status on CockroachDB | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VECTOR(384)`, `<=>` cosine distance | Supported natively; pgvector-compatible syntax. **Spike-confirmed** — `<->`/`<#>` too | `dedup.py`, `topic_match.py` |
| `CREATE EXTENSION vector` | ~~**Not supported**~~ **CORRECTED (task 0016): a no-op that SUCCEEDS on v26.2** — CockroachDB accepts `CREATE EXTENSION <anything>` as a compatibility shim. The line does not fail; a dialect guard is optional cleanup, not a blocker | `f49f90af49c0_initial_schema.py:27` |
| Vector *indexes* | L2 only; cosine is not index-accelerated | Moot — we have no vector index today |
| `DISTINCT ON` | Supported | `topics/service.py:184` |
| `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` | Supported | 12 call sites across `engagement`, `feed`, `notes` |
| `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` | Supported, BUT **spike found (task 0016)** it can skip a freshly-committed unlocked row in the write-intent resolution window. **Resolution:** the worker/quota claim transactions are short (lock → set `running` → commit in ms), so drop `SKIP LOCKED` for plain `FOR UPDATE` — a second pass blocks ms, then no-ops. Task 0019 step 0 | `worker/__main__.py:125`, `quota.py:1177` |
| Enums, `JSONB`, arrays, `BYTEA` | Supported. **Spike-confirmed** — plus `DISTINCT ON`, `ON CONFLICT`, partial/filtered UNIQUE indexes with `IN` predicates | throughout `domain/models/` |
| `asyncpg` async driver | Preliminary support via `sqlalchemy-cockroachdb` (`>=2.0.4,<2.1` — the dialect **caps SQLAlchemy `<2.1`**). **Spike-confirmed** the full query set runs | `core/db.py` |
| Serialization failures (`40001`) | **New failure mode** — the app must retry; Postgres never required this | every write path |

The last row is the real cost of this ADR, and the reason task 0019 exists as its own
piece of work rather than a footnote.

**The vector-index row is the pleasant surprise.** CockroachDB's vector indexes only
accelerate L2, and our similarity work is cosine — which would matter a great deal if
we had a vector index. We don't: `find_corpus_duplicate` scans within a single
`subtopic_id` (~20 rows), and topic matching scans the `topic` table (1,000 rows at
goal size). Both stay linear scans on either database, so nothing regresses.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- 1,000+ topics fits in the free tier. The stated product goal becomes reachable
  without a bill, which is the entire point.
- Custom user topics stop being a storage risk we have to ration for storage reasons
  (ADR-0003's per-user cap stays, but for *quota* reasons, which is what it was for).
- The migration is done at 46 MB, which is small enough to export, import, and verify
  by hand in a session.

**Harder**

- **A second meter.** Neon's free tier is storage-capped. CockroachDB Basic meters
  storage *and* Request Units (50M/month free). At the documented rate — ~1 RU per
  64-byte row plus 1 RU per additional KiB — a ~3.2 KB card costs ~5 RU to read, so a
  10-card feed page is ~50 RU and the monthly allowance is on the order of a million
  feed pages. Not a near-term constraint, but it is a ceiling that *did not previously
  exist*, and it is driven by traffic rather than content. Task 0021 instruments it.
- **Transaction retries become the application's problem.** Under `SERIALIZABLE`,
  CockroachDB returns `40001` and expects a client-side retry. Postgres, at our
  contention level, never made us think about this. Every write path inherits a new
  failure mode (task 0019).
- **We take on a dialect.** `sqlalchemy-cockroachdb`'s asyncpg support is described by
  its own maintainers as preliminary. That is a smaller, less-maintained dependency
  sitting under every query in the project.
- **Local dev and production diverge unless we make them not.** Running Postgres
  locally and CockroachDB in production would reintroduce exactly the class of bug this
  ADR is trying to price honestly. Task 0016 moves the local target too.

**Committed to**

- Free-tier limits are re-verified against current provider docs before the cutover
  (ADR-0003's standing commitment; the 10 GiB and 50M RU figures here were verified
  2026-08-22 and have a shelf life).
- The test suite runs against CockroachDB, not Postgres, once the cutover lands. A
  compatibility rule that is only true in production is not a rule, it is a hope —
  same principle as CLAUDE.md's "enforced twice, never documented once".

## Alternatives considered

**Stay on Neon and pay when it fills (ADR-0003's original answer).** The honest
default, and still the fallback if task 0016 fails. Lost because the user's constraint
is explicit and not a preference: *no payment before 1,000+ topics*. Neon's free tier
cannot reach a tenth of that. Paying is a fine engineering answer to a question that
was not being asked.

**Stack several Neon free accounts and shard the corpus across them (~2 GB).**
Rejected on two counts. It is against the spirit and likely the letter of free-tier
terms, which puts the database itself at risk of suspension. And it violates ADR-0003
§2 harder than anything else on this list: cross-shard routing for `card` + `question` +
`card_stats` + engagement, plus similarity search across shards, is real application
code written specifically to be deleted later. It still tops out at 2 GB — under half
the goal — so it buys a rewrite and *still* doesn't get there.

**Self-host the database on the owner's laptop.** A strictly worse version of the
always-free-VM option ADR-0003 already rejected: it adds sleep/reboot/network
availability to the failure modes, requires tunnelling to be reachable, and exposes a
database from home hardware that two people would have to patch and secure themselves.

**Prune content to fit 500 MB** — shorter cards, fewer per subtopic, archiving cold
topics. Rejected because it trades the product's actual substance for infrastructure
convenience. Coverage-based progression (ADR-0009) is defined against card counts;
thinning the corpus to fit a database tier would quietly change what "mastery" means.

**Supabase / PlanetScale / other free tiers.** Supabase's free tier caps at 500 MB
(same wall as Neon) and pauses idle projects. PlanetScale dropped its free tier
entirely and is MySQL, which costs us `JSONB`, arrays, enums, and vector support in one
move. Neither reaches 1,000 topics.

## Revisit when

- **Task 0016 fails.** If the stack cannot run on CockroachDB — dialect, vector type,
  or Alembic — this ADR is void and ADR-0003's paid-Neon path is the answer. Record
  that outcome rather than quietly abandoning the migration.
- **RU consumption crosses ~50% of the monthly allowance.** That means traffic, not
  content, has become the binding meter, and the tradeoff this ADR made (trading a
  storage ceiling for a storage-plus-traffic ceiling) has stopped paying.
- **Storage passes 8 GiB (~80%).** At the heavy-topic end that is roughly 900 topics —
  close enough to the goal that the next decision is "start paying", as originally
  planned in ADR-0003 §2.
- **Serialization retries show up as user-visible errors** rather than being absorbed
  by task 0019's retry boundary. That would mean the contention profile is worse than
  a low-write, corpus-read workload should produce, and is worth understanding before
  papering over.

adrs.title: ADR-0049: No message broker in v1; Kafka is rejected, not deferred-by-accident
adrs.summary: Rejecting a Kafka-based write-decoupling proposal — the queue already lives in Postgres and the premise was never measured.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0049: No message broker in v1; Kafka is rejected, not deferred-by-accident

- **Status:** Accepted (extends 0003 §4)
- **Date:** 2026-08-22
- **Deciders:** Anubhav

## Context

A proposal (2026-08-22) suggested moving Spoin's backend to an event-driven
architecture on Apache Kafka, alongside the CockroachDB migration that
[ADR-0048](/work/spoin#adr-0048) accepted. Concretely: `aiokafka` in the API,
domain events (`CardDwellEvent`, `CardSwipedEvent`, `QuizSubmittedEvent`) produced on
the request path, and a stream-consumer worker folding them into affinity scores.

This ADR exists because *rejecting* that is a decision with reasoning worth keeping.
ADR-0003 §4 already said "no Redis in v1" and explained why; without an equivalent
record here, "should we put Kafka in front of engagement writes?" is a question that
gets re-asked every few months and re-answered from scratch.

The proposal also framed Kafka as part of the fix for the storage ceiling. It is worth
saying explicitly that those are unrelated problems — a broker does not store a corpus,
and the storage ceiling is fully addressed by ADR-0048 on its own.

## Decision

**No message broker — Kafka or otherwise — in v1.** Engagement events continue to be
written directly to the database by `engagement/service.py`, and generation continues
to be driven by `GenerationJob` rows claimed by the batch worker (ADR-0003 §3).

The reasoning is the same shape as ADR-0003 §4's Redis argument, applied to the three
jobs a broker would take on here:

1. **A queue.** We have one: `GenerationJob` in Postgres, claimed with
   `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (`worker/__main__.py:125`), with priority ordering
   (ADR-0003 §6) and durability the database already guarantees. The workload it
   serves is bounded by free-tier LLM quota — order tens of jobs per day. A broker
   sized for millions of events per second is not the missing piece.

2. **Write decoupling for engagement.** The premise is that high-frequency engagement
   writes contend with transactional work. Nothing has measured that. Engagement rows
   are ~296 KB total across the entire live database, against 34 MB of content — the
   write path is not remotely the busy one, and `on_conflict_do_nothing` on an
   idempotency key already makes ingest cheap and retry-safe (ADR-0011). Optimizing an
   unmeasured bottleneck is how a project acquires a second database to operate.

3. **Async affinity/telemetry processing.** Real, and genuinely the strongest of the
   three — but ADR-0011's event/state/aggregate split already puts the seam there.
   Aggregates are derived from an append-only event log by a batch job. If that job
   becomes too slow or too coupled, the fix is to change what reads the log, not to
   put a broker in front of writing to it.

The load-bearing constraint is unchanged from ADR-0003: **the binding limit is LLM
generation quota, not throughput.** A swipe is ~50ms and an LLM call is 2–10 seconds.
Kafka makes the fast half faster.

### The cost side, stated plainly

- **A third stateful system to operate**, on a two-person team already responsible for
  a database and a worker — brokers, topics, partitions, consumer groups, offset
  management, rebalancing, dead-letter handling, and the failure modes each of those
  has at 3am.
- **A new class of bug**: at-least-once delivery, consumer lag, out-of-order events,
  and the reprocessing story after a bad deploy. ADR-0011's idempotency key helps, but
  only because it exists — the guarantee is currently "the write either happened or it
  didn't", and a broker replaces that with something weaker.
- **A serverless Kafka tier is metered per message**, which is exactly the failure
  ADR-0003 §4 named for Redis: a per-command meter that an idle polling consumer burns
  through while doing nothing.
- **It violates ADR-0003 §2.** Producing domain events from the request path is not a
  configuration change; removing the broker later would mean unwinding every producer
  call site. This is the "requires a rewrite to undo" category the whole free-tier
  strategy is built to avoid.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- The architecture stays two verticals over one database (CLAUDE.md's read path /
  write path split). A new session does not have to learn a streaming layer to change
  how a swipe is recorded.
- Engagement stays synchronously consistent: a swipe that returns 200 is durably
  recorded, full stop. No "eventually the aggregate catches up" caveat in the UI.

**Harder**

- If engagement volume genuinely does outgrow direct writes, we will be doing that
  migration under load rather than ahead of it. Accepted deliberately: the trigger
  condition is written into "Revisit when" below so the signal is not missed, and the
  event log's existing shape (ADR-0011) is what makes the migration tractable when it
  comes.
- Cross-service fan-out (multiple independent consumers of the same event) stays
  awkward. We have no second consumer today.

**Committed to**

- Anything that looks like a queue keeps living in Postgres until Postgres is measured
  to be the problem — same standard ADR-0003 §4 set for Redis.

## Alternatives considered

**Kafka for engagement telemetry only** (the proposal's narrower option). Lost on the
same measurement point: 296 KB of engagement data is not a decoupling problem. Also
the smaller scope does not shrink the operational cost much — you still run and monitor
a broker, you just use less of it.

**Kafka for the LLM generation pipeline.** Worse than the telemetry version. Generation
is tens of long-running jobs per day gated by a quota governor that deliberately
serializes calls per (key, model) cell (ADR-0040). Streaming buys throughput for a
workload whose entire design goal is *not* to go fast.

**Learn distributed systems on Spoin as the teaching vehicle** — the proposal's stated
"mastery" framing. A legitimate goal, and the reason this rejection is about placement
rather than merit. It lost because a production codebase serving real users is an
expensive classroom: every teaching artifact becomes something the next session has to
read, maintain, and reason around. A standalone sandbox teaches the same material with
no blast radius. Kept out of `docker-compose.yml` for that reason.

**Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` as a middle ground.** Not pursued, but genuinely the right
next rung *if* a decoupling need appears: it is additive, needs no new infrastructure,
and unwinds cleanly. Named here so the next person reaching for Kafka checks this
first.

## Revisit when

- **Engagement writes are measured** — not assumed — to be contending with the feed
  read path, or ingest latency shows up in the ~50ms swipe budget (ADR-0010).
- **A second independent consumer of the engagement log exists.** One consumer is a
  batch job; three is a bus, and at three the broker starts paying for itself.
- **The batch aggregate job cannot keep up**, such that users see stale progress for
  long enough to notice. Check whether the fix is a better reader first.
- **Generation stops being quota-bound** (ADR-0003's "traction arrives" trigger). If
  generation throughput is ever limited by our own orchestration rather than by the
  provider's request ceiling, the queue assumptions in §1 above are worth re-reading.

adrs.title: ADR-0050: Being shown a card consumes it; a difficulty turns over instead of running dry
adrs.summary: Fixing a feed that could show the same slate forever: an impression now marks a card deferred and actually drives the difficulty cycle forward.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0050: Being shown a card consumes it; a difficulty turns over instead of running dry

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Deciders:** mayanks0ni
- **Amends:** [ADR-0010](/work/spoin#adr-0010) — "scrolling past never counts" now
  applies to *progression* only. It no longer means an impression changes nothing.
- **Fixes a drift from:** [ADR-0010](/work/spoin#adr-0010), whose own seen-state
  section already specified "the cycle advances when no `UNSEEN` cards remain at that
  difficulty across all subtopics". Nothing ever implemented that sentence.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0054](/work/spoin#adr-0054)
  -- `FeedPage.starved`'s "gains a consumer" revisit condition below is answered in the
  opposite direction: a single-topic filter running dry now recycles instead of ever
  reaching the starved path, so the demand-driven fill loop stays exactly as half-wired
  as it was here, just less visibly.

## Context

A reader who scrolled without opening anything was served the same cards forever.

Three separate gaps produced it, and each one alone would have been enough:

1. **An impression changed nothing.** `_apply_state`'s `IMPRESSION` branch wrote
   `UNSEEN` — the state the card was already in — under the comment "scrolling past
   never counts". So a card stayed eligible no matter how many times it had been
   shown. Nothing but deliberate reading ever consumed one.

2. **The cycle counter had no writer.** `UserTopicCycle` was read in two places and
   written in none, anywhere in the codebase. `cycle` was therefore permanently `0`,
   `deferred_cycle` was permanently `0`, and ADR-0010's eligibility rule
   `deferred_cycle < current_cycle` evaluated `0 < 0` — false, always. The
   second-chance pass could not happen even in principle. The model's own docstring
   promised the behaviour; no code delivered it.

3. **Nothing ever deferred a card.** The only kind reaching `_defer` was `SKIP`, and
   the client never emits it — `"skip"` exists solely as a member of the
   `EngagementKind` union in `lib/api.ts`, referenced by no component.

ADR-0010 anticipated exactly this failure and said so plainly: *"Deferred-card
cycling is genuinely fiddly and needs real test coverage. A bug here shows as 'I keep
seeing the same cards', which is the most damaging feed bug there is."*

There **was** a test. `test_deferred_cards_return_only_after_the_cycle_advances`
passed because it inserted `UserTopicCycle(cycle=1)` by hand, with the comment
"advance the cycle, as the worker does once no UNSEEN cards remain." No worker did.
The test supplied the one piece of state production code never produced, and so
proved the half of the mechanism that worked while hiding the half that did not.

The product consequence: Spoin is meant to be scrollable the way a social feed is,
where reading is opt-in. A feed that can only advance for someone who reads is a
feed that stalls for its most common visitor.

## Decision

**Being shown a card consumes it. Reading a card is what counts.** Those become two
different things.

- **An impression marks the card `DEFERRED`**, not `UNSEEN`. It leaves rotation until
  the difficulty turns over.
- **The client only emits an impression after 1000ms of continuous ≥50% visibility.**
  An impression now costs the reader a card, so it has to be earned; without a
  threshold one fast flick down the feed would burn everything it passed.
- **`_maybe_advance_cycle` implements ADR-0010's sentence.** A difficulty turns over
  when **no `UNSEEN` remain** *and* **something is actually deferred**. Both
  conditions are load-bearing: advancing with nothing deferred would quietly paper
  over a starved pool that should be reported and generated into instead. It runs
  only when a stratum comes back empty — two `EXISTS` queries on a path that was
  about to serve nothing.
- **A repeat pass shuffles rather than ranks.** By the second pass `coverage_need` is
  ~0 everywhere and quality/recency would hand back the same order every cycle,
  making a re-read feel like a replay. `diversify` still applies, so one subtopic
  cannot clump.
- **The repeat is announced once**, via a `recycling` flag on the feed response. An
  unexplained repeat reads as a bug, and ADR-0006 is explicit that these states are a
  design surface rather than an error path.

**`DEFERRED` stays out of progression.** `_bump_subtopic_progress` counts
`state == SEEN` exclusively, so being shown a card advances the 80% coverage gate by
exactly nothing. ADR-0010's "speed-swiping earns nothing" is preserved in the sense
that matters: scrolling gets you an endless feed, never a quiz unlock.

## Consequences

**Easier**

- The feed advances for a reader who does not read, which is the behaviour the
  product was always described as having.
- ADR-0010's three-state model finally behaves as written, so the ADR can be trusted
  as a description of the system rather than of an intention.
- "I keep seeing the same cards" stops being reachable through the common path.

**Harder**

- An impression is now destructive, so its threshold is a real tuning parameter with
  a bad failure mode on each side. Too low and a scroll burns a slate; too high and
  the feed stalls again. 1000ms is a starting point, not a measured value.
- Cards genuinely repeat now. Duplicate suppression on the client had to be narrowed
  from "every card this session" to a 40-card window — the session-wide version would
  have swallowed the entire repeat pass and reported the feed exhausted at the exact
  moment it finally had more to give. That window is now the thing standing between a
  legitimate repeat and the adjacent-duplicate bug, and it is a heuristic.
- Read cards never return. A reader who genuinely finishes a difficulty still runs
  out, and only a quiz moves them up. This ADR does not address that.

**Committed to**

- Coverage counts `SEEN` and nothing else. Any future state that also implies
  "the reader engaged" must not be folded into that count without its own ADR.
- A difficulty turns over only when something is waiting to be released. Turning over
  an empty difficulty would hide starvation.
- Any test asserting the cycle behaviour drives it through the service. Writing
  `UserTopicCycle` directly from a test is what let this bug live.

## Alternatives considered

**Recycle `SEEN` cards too, once the deferred pile is also drained.** The literal
reading of "repeat them all once the difficulty is finished", and rejected for now.
`SEEN` is load-bearing for the 80% gate and `UserSubtopicProgress.seen_count`;
returning those cards to rotation means either double-counting coverage or teaching
every counter to ignore repeats. Since a scroller marks almost nothing `SEEN`, the
deferred pile alone already delivers the endless feed. Revisit if readers who
*do* read start hitting the wall.

**Mark a card consumed the moment it is served, in `build_slate`.** Simplest possible
rule and no client change. Rejected: serving is not seeing. A card at the bottom of a
page the reader never scrolls to would be burned unseen, and the reader would never
know what they missed.

**Advance the cycle from a batch job**, as the old test's comment imagined. Rejected:
it puts a user-visible latency between "ran out" and "has more", for a decision that
is one `EXISTS` query on a path already known to be empty. Nothing about it needs to
be asynchronous.

**Key the difficulty-mix ramp off cards shown rather than cards read.** Considered
and deliberately not done. `dynamic_mix` holds a reader at 100% of their own tier
until they have read 20% of it, so a scroller never sees the 20% intermediate slice.
Loosening that would hand people harder cards they have no grounding in, which is the
ramp's entire purpose — and since tier promotion requires passing a quiz, a scroller
stays at their tier regardless. Left alone until the simpler fix has been felt.

## Revisit when

- Readers who actually read report running out. That is the signal the `SEEN`
  alternative above is now worth its complexity.
- The 1000ms impression threshold is measured against real scroll behaviour rather
  than assumed. Either failure mode showing up in engagement data should move it.
- `FeedPage.starved` gains a consumer. It currently has none — the router drops it
  and no fill job is enqueued from a starved read, so ADR-0006's demand-driven fill
  loop is only half-wired. Recycling keeps the feed moving over a corpus that is too
  small, which makes that gap easier to ignore and more important to close.

adrs.title: ADR-0051: A "no color" opt-out for per-topic accent, via a sentinel hue
adrs.summary: Adding a third accent state so a topic can opt out of color tinting entirely, alongside the deterministic-default and chosen-hue states.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0051: A "no color" opt-out for per-topic accent, via a sentinel hue

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-22
- **Deciders:** Anubhav
- **Amends:** [ADR-0034](/work/spoin#adr-0034) -- `UserTopic.accent_hue`
  gains a third meaning for the same column; no new field.

## Context

ADR-0034 gave `UserTopic.accent_hue` two states: `null` ("use the deterministic
default hue") and `0-359` ("use this hue"). Every topic renders tinted, one way or
another -- there was no way to say "don't tint this topic at all, just use the
palette's own accent," which is exactly what `--topic-accent` already falls back to
whenever a card sets no `--topic-hue` (`globals.css`'s `--topic-accent: var(--accent)`
base case). That fallback already existed structurally; nothing exposed it as a user
choice.

The request is a "no color" option in the existing swatch picker (`TopicStatsModal`)
that lands on this fallback deliberately, for users who find per-topic tinting noisy
in a mixed feed or simply prefer every card to read as "this palette," unmodified.

## Decision

**A third state on the same `accent_hue` column, via the sentinel `-1` --
`NO_TOPIC_COLOR` in `lib/topicColor.ts`.** No migration: the column is already a plain
nullable `Integer` with no `CHECK` constraint, so a third meaning costs nothing on the
schema. `TopicColorIn.hue`'s validator widens from `ge=0` to `ge=-1`.

**All three states, spelled out:**

| `accent_hue` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `null` | Use the deterministic default hue (ADR-0034) |
| `0-359` | Use this hue |
| `-1` (`NO_TOPIC_COLOR`) | Opt out -- render the palette's plain `--accent`, no `--topic-hue` set |

**`topicHue()` is the only place that interprets the sentinel.** It now returns
`number | null` instead of a bare `number`: `null` means "set no `--topic-hue`," which
every consumer already needs to handle correctly (Card.tsx's expanded border, hero
ring, `.card-topic`, saved tiles) since that's the same shape `--topic-accent`'s CSS
fallback already expects. Three call sites (`SavedView`, `LikedView`, `NotesView`'s
collection-filter chips) were reading `UserTopic.accent_hue` directly off the wire
instead of through `topicHue()` -- those are the ones a sentinel would silently break,
rendering `-1` as a red-ish hue via `oklch(from var(--accent) l c -1deg)` instead of no
color at all. They're moved onto a new `explicitTopicHue()`, which was already their
actual intent (tint only on an explicitly chosen hue, never the computed default) --
the opt-out state and "never colored, no default shown" were already indistinguishable
there before this change, and stay that way, which is correct for a chip meant to
label an actively-chosen color.

**No new picker widget.** The existing 8-swatch row in `TopicStatsModal` (ADR-0034's
"discrete swatches, not a continuous wheel" pattern) gains a 9th control: filled with
the plain `--accent` (honest -- that's exactly what selecting it renders) with a
diagonal slash overlay, the conventional "no fill" affordance distinguishing it from a
hue choice rather than looking like one more color.

## Consequences

**Easier**
- Zero schema changes; the whole feature is a validator range widen, a client-side
  sentinel constant, and a picker button.
- A user who finds mixed-feed tinting noisy can turn it off per topic without losing
  the ability to turn it back on (still stores a real value, just a specific one).

**Harder**
- `accent_hue`'s three-state meaning now lives only in code comments and this ADR, not
  in the type system -- `number | null` on the wire doesn't distinguish "a hue" from
  "the opt-out sentinel." A reviewer unfamiliar with this ADR could reasonably read
  `-1` as a bug. Mitigated by requiring every read to route through `topicHue()`/
  `explicitTopicHue()` rather than reading `accent_hue` raw, with a comment on the
  field pointing here.

## Alternatives considered

**A second boolean column (`color_enabled` or similar).** Rejected: makes the pair a
two-column invariant (a `hue` alongside an `enabled` that can disagree) for a state
that fits in the existing nullable int's unused negative range, and would have needed
a migration `set_color` and every reader don't otherwise need.

**Redefine `null` as "no color" and always materialize a real hue at subscribe time.**
The cleanest data model in isolation, but it inverts ADR-0034's whole point --
`null`'s value *is* "compute the default lazily, no write needed just to have one."
Redefining it would also mean a backfill `UPDATE` across every existing `UserTopic`
row in `spoin_db`, which CLAUDE.md gates behind the project owner's explicit approval
even framed as routine maintenance. Rejected without asking, since the sentinel
achieves the same user-facing result with no data migration at all.

## Revisit when

If a topic-level (not per-user) "no color" default is ever wanted -- e.g. an
editorially flagged topic that should never tint regardless of who's viewing --
that's a `Topic`-level field the same way ADR-0034's "Revisit when" describes for a
shared accent color, with `UserTopic.accent_hue` still taking precedence when set
(including the sentinel).

adrs.title: ADR-0052: A single-slot undo toast for removal in Notes/Liked/Saved
adrs.summary: A 5-second undo toast for removing notes, likes, and bookmarks, plus a cross-view store fixing stale liked/bookmarked state.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0052: A single-slot undo toast for removal in Notes/Liked/Saved

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-22
- **Deciders:** Anubhav

## Context

Removing a card from Notes, Liked, or Saved was already a one-click, no-confirmation
action -- consistent with those views' optimistic-update pattern (unlike/unbookmark/
delete-note all update local state immediately, before the server round-trip
resolves). Nothing softened an accidental removal. The request is an undo affordance:
a bottom toast, live for 5 seconds, dismissible early via an X.

Two things make this more than "add a toast":

1. **The three "remove" actions are not the same operation.** Unliking and
   unbookmarking are hard `DELETE`s of `CardLike`/`CardBookmark` rows
   ([engagement/service.py](../../apps/api/src/spoin/engagement/service.py)).
   Deleting a note is `DELETE /cards/{id}/note`. There is no shared "soft delete" or
   "trash" concept anywhere in this schema to lean on (CLAUDE.md is explicit that
   `spoin_db` has none, and inventing one for this alone would be a parallel
   mechanism for a five-second convenience).
2. **Every collection view stays mounted-but-hidden once visited**
   (`AppShell`'s `visited` set, `hidden` attribute, never unmounted) so switching
   from Liked to Notes mid-countdown must not lose the toast. A toast owned by the
   view that triggered it would disappear the moment its subtree goes `hidden`.

## Decision

**Delete immediately; undo re-creates, it does not un-delete.** Each view captures
the full row it's about to drop from its own already-in-memory `rows` state, filters
it out (unchanged optimistic-update behavior), and hands the captured row to
`offerUndo()`. Undo re-issues the *original* mutating call -- `engagement.record(id,
"like")`, `engagement.record(id, "bookmark")`, or `api.saveNote(id, body)` -- and
re-inserts the row into local state. No new "pending delete" state, no deferred
write: the row is genuinely gone and genuinely restorable, the same way a real user
action would redo it.

**The honest cost this accepts: undo is a fresh row, not a reversal.** A re-liked
card gets a new `CardLike.created_at`; a restored note gets a new `updated_at`. Both
surface in "RECENT" sort order jumping the item to the top. This was chosen over
inventing soft-delete specifically to avoid a second schema concept for a UI
convenience -- see Alternatives.

**One undo slot, newest wins -- `lib/undo.ts`, a module-level store mirroring
`lib/refresh.ts`'s pub/sub shape** (this codebase's existing pattern for
"one piece of client state several disconnected components need to see and react
to"). `offerUndo()` replaces whatever offer is currently live and restarts its
5-second timer; there is no queue. Removing a second card while the first's toast is
still showing makes the first item permanently gone -- deliberately, matching how
Gmail's archive/delete toast behaves, rather than turning a lightweight affordance
into a list the user has to triage.

**One toast component, mounted once in `AppShell`, outside every view's subtree.**
`UndoToast` subscribes to the store and renders fixed-position, bottom-center,
`z-index: 120` (above the Saved-card overlay's `z-index: 100`, below the custom
cursor's `999`). This is what makes "switch views mid-countdown, toast survives"
work at all -- a toast rendered inside `LikedView`'s own tree would vanish under
`hidden` the instant the user navigates away.

**The X dismisses; it does not undo.** Clicking it calls `dismissUndo()`, which
clears the timer and the slot -- the removal already happened and stays that way.
This is worth stating because "X" on a toast is occasionally misread as "cancel the
action" rather than "stop offering to reverse it."

**`role="status"` / `aria-live="polite"`, not a focus-stealing dialog.** The toast
announces itself to assistive tech without interrupting whatever the user is doing,
consistent with how `GuestNotice` (the only other standing toast-like surface) is
built.

## Consequences

**Easier**
- Every "remove" action across the three views gets undo with the same ~15-line
  shape: capture row → filter → `offerUndo`. No new API endpoints, no schema
  changes.
- The store is view-agnostic; extending undo to the feed's like/bookmark toggle or
  to unfollowing a topic later is a call to `offerUndo`, not new infrastructure.

**Harder**
- `accent_hue`-style "one true value" reasoning doesn't apply here: the event log
  now honestly contains like → unlike → like sequences from a single accidental tap
  + undo, which is correct under ADR-0011's event/state/aggregate separation but is
  a fact worth knowing before reading engagement events as literal user intent.
- A 5-second window is short for a screen-reader or keyboard user to react to a live
  region and act before it disappears (WCAG 2.2.1 is stricter than this). Accepted
  because the removal is already committed -- the timeout only withdraws a
  convenience, it never destroys data outright, and the requested behavior was
  explicit about the 5-second figure.
- Restoring a row inserts it at the front of the client's in-memory list rather than
  recomputing where the active sort (`recent`/`oldest`/`topic`/`difficulty`) would
  actually place it -- all three sorts are server-side (`api.likedCards`/
  `savedCards`/`listNotes` take the sort key), so an exact client-side re-sort would
  duplicate that logic. The next natural refetch (the same `invalidate()` call each
  original removal already triggers) corrects the position.

## Alternatives considered

**A real soft-delete / trash table**, restorable without a new write. Rejected:
introduces a schema concept (`deleted_at` or a trash table) that nothing else in
this codebase has, for a five-second UI convenience -- the kind of thing CLAUDE.md's
"anything that must be *true* is enforced outside the model" framing would call
over-engineering in the other direction: adding a durable mechanism for a transient
UI state.

**Deferring the actual `DELETE`/`unlike` call until the 5 seconds elapse**, so undo
is simply "never send it." Rejected: `unlike`/`unbookmark` are in
`engagement.ts`'s `URGENT` set specifically because progression-adjacent state
should not sit unflushed client-side; a 5-second hold before *any* write would
invert that guarantee, and the row would need to be faked as already-removed in the
UI regardless, so nothing about this decision gets simpler.

**A toast queue** instead of a single replaced slot. Rejected: turns "quick
convenience if you misclick" into a small triage UI for anyone removing several
things in a row, which is the more common case (batch-cleaning Saved) this feature
is least useful for anyway.

## Revisit when

- If undo is wanted for the feed's own like/bookmark toggle, or for unfollowing a
  topic, `offerUndo`/`UndoToast` already generalize -- no redesign needed, just a
  new call site.
- If the 5-second window turns out to be a real accessibility complaint in practice
  (not hypothetical), lengthen it or pause the timer on focus/hover before reaching
  for a queue or a differently-shaped affordance.

adrs.title: ADR-0087: `frog` is a sibling package that owns the embedder
adrs.summary: Retrieval moves into its own importable package that spoin depends on, never the reverse, so the boundary is structural rather than decorative.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0087: `frog` is a sibling Python package that owns the embedder; `spoin` depends on it, never the reverse

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-04
- **Deciders:** project owner, implementing session
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0092](/work/spoin#adr-0092) — the
  embedder becomes `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` at 1024 dimensions, and the `Embedder`
  interface becomes asymmetric. This ADR's "vectors stay 384-dim" no longer holds.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0097](/work/spoin#adr-0097) — `spoin_db_2`'s
  columns move to 1024 too, so the "same space" this ADR committed to is restored at
  the new number. Every "384" below reads as 1024.
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0093](/work/spoin#adr-0093) —
  `normalize_topic_text` moves into `frog` after all. The "stays in `spoin`" clause below
  no longer holds; it was written before ADR-0088 gave the function a caller on the far
  side of a boundary frog cannot cross.

## Context

[Task 0038](../tasks/0038-frog-rag-and-hybrid-generation.md) commits us to
retrieval-grounded generation. Three facts force the shape of the thing that does
the retrieving.

**We are about to draft on small models.** The [mistral-saga](../mistral-saga/README.md)
established that this account's only usable Mistral models are `ministral-3b/8b/14b`
and `codestral` — no reasoning-capable model at any tier. A 3B model's parametric
recall is not something the product's "quiz-gated mastery of true things" claim can
rest on. The facts have to come from a corpus.

**Retrieval happens several times per generation call.** The planner retrieves, the
writer retrieves, the verification pass retrieves against the same material. An HTTP
hop per retrieval buys nothing and adds both latency and a failure mode to a path
that is already fighting for calls/minute.

**We already have an embedder, and it is in the wrong place for this.**
`spoin.embeddings` provides `get_embedder()` — local, never quota'd (hard rule 5),
`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` at 384 dimensions, with a deterministic `HashEmbedder`
stand-in so the stack boots without `onnxruntime`. A retrieval package needs that
embedder. If the retrieval package lives outside `spoin` and imports it from
`spoin`, the dependency runs in both directions and the boundary is decorative.

## Decision

**`frog` is a separate importable Python package at `apps/frog/`, with its own
`pyproject.toml`. It is a library, not a service. `apps/api` takes a path dependency
on it. `frog` must not import `spoin`.**

`apps/helpers/` is the precedent for a non-service sibling, though it has no
`pyproject.toml` and is not importable; frog needs both.

### frog owns the embedder classes; `spoin` keeps the factory

`Embedder`, `HashEmbedder` and `FastEmbedEmbedder` move into `frog.embeddings` as
**pure classes taking explicit parameters**. `spoin.embeddings.get_embedder()`
stays where it is, keeps reading `spoin.core.config`, and constructs a frog class.

This split is deliberate and is the only part of the move that is not mechanical.
The alternative — moving the factory too — requires frog to grow its own settings
object reading the same environment variables. `embedding_dim` configured in two
places is a silent-failure generator: a divergence produces vectors that are not
comparable, and nothing raises. Corpus chunk vectors and existing
`card.content_embedding` vectors must remain in the same space, so **384 dimensions
and the same model are load-bearing, not a default**.

~~`normalize_topic_text` stays in `spoin`. It is topic-canonicalization logic that
happens to be applied before embedding, not embedding infrastructure — task 0001's
threshold calibration depends on it not drifting, and that concern is spoin's.~~

**Superseded by [ADR-0093](/work/spoin#adr-0093)** (2026-09-05).
The clause above held only until something needed to call the function from frog's side.
ADR-0088's ingester does, and ADR-0088's own reasoning — *one* normalizer, so corpus tags
and canonical topic names cannot become two vocabularies — made duplicating it the wrong
answer. Unlike `get_embedder()`, it reads no settings, so there was nothing for a second
home to diverge about except the code.

### All 23 import sites are rewritten, no re-export shim

`spoin.embeddings` does not re-export frog's classes. Every call site that wants an
`Embedder` type imports it from `frog.embeddings`. A shim would make the boundary
invisible at exactly the places a reader needs to see it, and would accrete code —
CLAUDE.md's "a rule stated only in a doc is a wish".

### The boundary is enforced twice

Per CLAUDE.md's rule that a hard architectural rule gets enforced twice, never
documented once — the same wiring ADR-0002 uses to confine LangChain:

1. A `ruff` `banned-api` entry in `apps/frog/pyproject.toml` on `spoin`.
2. An AST-level check in `apps/api/tests/test_architecture.py` that walks
   `apps/frog`'s source and fails on any `spoin` import. It lives beside the
   existing boundary checks because that file is where someone auditing
   architectural rules already looks.

`make check` runs `ruff` and `mypy --strict` over `apps/frog` as well as `apps/api`.
frog gets its own `tests/` directory for unit tests of its own machinery
(the embedder, chunking, retrieval), run in the same `make test` pass.

### The Docker build context moves to the repository root

`apps/api/Dockerfile` currently builds with context `./apps/api` and `COPY src ./src`.
That context cannot reach `../frog`. The `api`, `seed`, `worker` and `test` services
move to `context: .` with `dockerfile: apps/api/Dockerfile`, copying both
`apps/frog` and `apps/api/src`.

This is the real cost of the sibling-package choice and task 0038 flagged it as such.
We are paying it rather than layering badly.

## Consequences

**Easier.** The dependency direction is a fact of the filesystem, not a convention.
frog can be tested, type-checked and reasoned about without the API. A future
consumer — `content/ascii_library.py`'s hand-rolled cosine search is the obvious
first candidate — sits on frog without importing anything from the generation stack.
`the_spoin_universe` gets a natural owner ([ADR-0088](/work/spoin#adr-0088)).

**Harder.** Four compose services change build context, which is a rebuild for
everyone and a class of path bug that only shows up in the image, not locally. A
change touching both packages is now two `pyproject.toml` files and two lint
configurations. The embedder split means a reader has to know that the classes and
the factory live in different packages — mitigated by a docstring in each pointing
at the other and at this ADR.

**Committed to.** 384-dimension vectors from `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, in both
databases, indefinitely. Changing the embedding model is now a two-database
re-embedding, not a config flip.

## Alternatives considered

**`apps/api/src/spoin/frog/` — a package inside `spoin`.** Task 0038 names this as
the fallback if packaging proves disproportionate. It needs no Docker changes at all.
It loses the thing the whole decision is for: inside `spoin`, frog *can* import
`spoin`, and the only thing stopping it is a lint rule on a package that has every
reason to reach for `spoin.core.config`. The boundary would be a wish. Kept as an
explicit fallback: if the build-context change proves worse than budgeted, this is
where we retreat to, and this ADR gets superseded rather than quietly ignored.

**frog as an HTTP service.** Rejected on the retrieval-frequency argument above.
Several retrievals per generation call, each a network hop with its own timeout and
its own failure mode, on a path whose entire history is a fight for throughput.

**Leave the embedder in `spoin`, have frog import it.** This is the inversion the
decision exists to prevent. `api → frog` and `frog → api` simultaneously means
neither package can be built, tested or reasoned about alone.

**Move the factory into frog too.** Rejected on the `embedding_dim`-drift argument:
two settings objects reading the same environment variable is a silent
incomparable-vectors bug waiting for someone to change one of them.

## Revisit when

- The Docker/CI cost of the sibling package exceeds what was budgeted — retreat to
  `spoin.frog`, supersede this.
- A second consumer of frog appears that is not in this repository. That is the
  signal that "library, not service" has stopped being right, and the retrieval-
  frequency argument should be re-measured rather than re-assumed.
- The embedding model changes. That is a two-database migration and deserves its own
  ADR.

adrs.title: ADR-0088: `the_spoin_universe` is a separate database with its own alembic environment
adrs.summary: The authored corpus lives in its own database whose migration environment never reads the production URL, so a corpus revision cannot land on user data.
adrs.content:
# ADR-0088: `the_spoin_universe` is a separate database with its own alembic environment; retrieval is cross-topic by default

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-04
- **Deciders:** project owner, implementing session
- **Amended by:** [ADR-0091](/work/spoin#adr-0091) — `document` gains
  `category`, `sub_category` and `scope`. The schema table below predates them.

## Context

[ADR-0087](/work/spoin#adr-0087) established `frog` as the retrieval
package. It needs somewhere to keep the source-of-truth corpus that
[task 0038](../tasks/0038-frog-rag-and-hybrid-generation.md) is built around.

The corpus is not application data. It is authored material — curated, revised, and
re-delivered repeatedly by an externally-owned track (Antigravity, supervised by the
owner). Its lifecycle, its backup requirements and its blast radius are all different
from `spoin_db_2`'s. Mixing authored reference material into the database that holds
users, cards and engagement events means every corpus revision is a migration against
production.

## Decision

**The corpus lives in `the_spoin_universe`, a separate database in the same Postgres
instance, with its own alembic environment owned by `frog`. Retrieval is cross-topic
by default.**

### ⚠️ The volume prohibition now protects three databases

`the_spoin_universe` shares the `db-data` volume with `spoin_db_2` and
`spoin_db_test`. CLAUDE.md's standing prohibition on `docker compose down -v`,
`make clean` and `docker volume rm` is unchanged and now costs more when violated.
Creating a database is non-destructive and does not relax anything.

### The alembic environment lives in `apps/frog/`, not `apps/api/`

`apps/api/alembic.ini` points at `SPOIN_DATABASE_URL`. frog gets its own
`apps/frog/alembic.ini` and `apps/frog/alembic/`, whose `env.py` reads
**`SPOIN_UNIVERSE_DATABASE_URL` and nothing else**.

This is the point of the choice, and it is a structural guarantee rather than a
convention: a universe migration cannot land on `spoin_db_2` because the environment
that runs it never reads the variable that names `spoin_db_2`. Two alembic
environments sharing a directory tree is precisely how a migration ends up on the
wrong database, which is a failure this project has paid for four times in a
neighbouring form.

Cost: a second compose service to run universe migrations, and `make migrate` /
`make migration` grow a universe counterpart.

### Schema

Two tables. Every column below is a decision, not a placeholder.

**`document`** — one authored source file.

| Column | Notes |
|---|---|
| `id` | UUID primary key |
| `source` | NOT NULL. URL or origin. Where the material came from. |
| `title` | NOT NULL. |
| `kind` | NOT NULL, Postgres enum: `spoin_canon` or `topic_source`. |
| `source_path` | NOT NULL, UNIQUE. Path within the delivered corpus; the document's identity. |
| `content_hash` | NOT NULL. sha256 of the raw file. Drives idempotent re-ingestion. |
| `source_date` | Nullable. When the *source material* is from — distinct from `ingested_at`. |
| `ingested_at` | NOT NULL. When we read it. |

**`chunk`** — a retrievable span of one document.

| Column | Notes |
|---|---|
| `id` | UUID primary key |
| `document_id` | FK to `document`, `ondelete=CASCADE` |
